ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS Mr. Stan J. Hovdebo (Prince Albert) moved:
That this House recognizes the tremendous financial difficulty that farmers have been placed under and therefore recommends that the government immediately consider injection of much needed cash into farming through:
(1)	the immediate payout of a substantial initial payment from the Western Grain Stabilization Fund in order to assist with seeding costs;
(2)	the repeal of all sales taxes, well-head taxes and other taxes being charged to fuels used for farming and fishing; and
(3)	an immediate interest rate reduction on Farm Credit Corporation loans so that viable refinancing of farms can take place.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the situation for farmers in Canada is so critical that my Party has decided to take the time of Parliament once again to try to convince the Government that it should take some action in the farming area. This is the third day that we have debated agricultural issues in the last month or so. We hope in the process of repeating that possibly the Government might learn something. We hope that government members are not the slow learners they appear to be.
The motion before the House is an attempt to point out to the Government that it has some responsibilities and that there are some areas to which it can react and act very quickly. The three points that we chose as possible methods of injecting funds into farming are as follows. First is the one about which we have been talking for the last year or so, the triggering of the Western Grain Stabilization Fund. The second is a rebate or repeal of the taxes on farm fuel. The third is a reduction in the interest rates of the Farm Credit Corporation which would
help some farmers who happen to fall into that particular category.
There are many other ways in which the Government could inject cash into the farm economy. However, what we have chosen to emphasize are only three ways in which the Liberal Government could act now and immediately inject funds into the agricultural industry and therefore have some immediate benefit. The Government could proceed with these changes this week or next week. Although for many farmers it would be too little and too late, it would provide relief for some.

I want to quote from the Catholic Bishops Ethical Reflections on the Economic Crisis. This paper was reinforced by the Bishops recently in a statement to the Macdonald Commission. It reads as follows:
-we firmly believe that first priority must be given to the real victims of the current recession, namely-the unemployed, the welfare poor, the working poor-pensioners, native peoples, women, young people-and small farmers, fishermen, some factory workers, and some small businessmen and women. This option calls for economic policies which realize that the needs of the poor have priority over the wants of the rich; that the rights of the workers are more important than the maximization of profits; that the participation of marginalized groups takes precedence over the preservation of a system which excludes them.
It is difficult to believe that I am making that quotation refer to the prairie farmers and other Canadian farmers. Farming is the number one industry in Canada. This Government has allowed it to slip to the point where many farmers are disappearing from farming entirely. They are on the poor end of the economy.
Recognizing the farmers as a marginal group is a real shock to those of us who grew up close to the farming industry. We have to credit this to the unconcern of this Government and its lack of understanding of the farming industry. It is not only the grain producers but farmers all across Canada who feel this neglect by the Government.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) will probably stand in his place and tell us that the Canadian farmer is better off than farmers anywhere else in the world. That may be so, but he will be misrepresenting the situation on the farm these days for many farmers. In 1979 there were 124 farm bankruptcies in Canada. In 1983 this had increased to 488 bankruptcies, an increase of over 250 per cent. Comparing January and February of 1984 with January and February of 1983, there was a 63 per cent increase across this country. In the west there was more than a 100 per cent increase in bankruptcies.
Anyone who knows the farm situation recognizes that bankruptcies are only the tip of the iceberg. The Canadian Federa-

tion of Agriculture states that for every farmer who goes bankrupt, there are 10 in trouble or who will pack their bags and leave the farm. During the last five years, close to 20,000 farms have disappeared. I challenge the Minister of Agriculture to state that that is good for agriculture and good for Canada.
This motion contains some very simple proposals which can be put into effect immediately. First, it proposes an insured pay-out from the Western Grain Stabilization Fund. It proposes that the Government make that pay-out now and not at election time. I know the Minister will tell us that that cannot be done, but where there is a will there is a way. As was suggested by the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) yesterday, the Minister could make an interim payment. We are told that that has been done before.
The Minister could put the enabling legislation before the House. In the last two years since we have known that the triggering system did not work very well, the Minister has had enough time to do so. He could put the enabling legislation before the House now and have it passed as quickly as possible. If he would propose a Bill which would be honest, above-board and do what it is supposed to do, it would have our support. However, we will not buy a pig in a poke. Such a Bill could contain a triggering system which would be retroactive to the last calendar year and the initial payments could then be made for the 1983 calendar year, with a final payment if necessary at the end of this crop year.
Let us not allow the Minister or the Government to use such a Bill as a lever to get less palatable Bills through the House simply because opposition members want the Bill passed quickly and are more concerned about farmers than the Government. Let us not hear government members say: "We will pass this Bill if you will pass some of the others". These kinds of shenanigans are evidence of the low priority the Government gives to farmers' problems. After having witnessed the promising Liberal leadership contenders invade Saskatchewan last week, such shenanigans would show a great deal of contempt for Saskatchewan.
The Minister has made a great to-do about where the money for these projected pay-outs would come from. The last payout from the Western Grain Stabilization Fund was made in 1978. Since that time farmers have put $300 million into the fund. The Government has committed $600 million to the fund but it has never had to find that money. Not one cent of the payment which the Government is now suggesting would come directly from the Government. In the accounts of Canada I cannot find anywhere an item indicating that the Government has actually paid that money into the account. The Government has made paper transactions by theoretically putting money into a trust fund and then borrowing it back. The Government has never had to pay any money out and it would not have to pay any money out if it made a payment right now. Unfortunately, even if farmers were to receive a payment from the Western Grain Stabilization Fund, it would be too little, too late for many beginning farmers.
The second proposal contained in our motion is the repeal of taxes on farm fuels. Farmers will spend approximately $1.5 million on farm fuel this year and because of the recent increases it may be considerably more than that. That figure does not include the energy that is used to produce fertilizer, another large portion of the costs of farming these days. Of the cost of farming, upward of 20 per cent is made up of taxes which are put in place by the federal Government. If the Government had a great desire to help farmers, it would do something immediately for the primary producers like farmers or fishermen. However, in this particular motion we are more interested in the farmers. The Government could reduce by 32 cents per gallon-approximately 7 cents per litre-the cost of fuel. That would be a reduction in fuel costs of approximately 20 per cent. Farmers who use a considerable amount of fuel would be helped by $1,000, or more in their costs. For every thousand gallons of fuel that farmers bought, they would save $300. That is a sizeable injection of cash into the farming industry.
The third area of concern that is brought forward in the motion is the matter of the interest rates of the Farm Credit Corporation. This would help a few farmers who have Farm Credit Corporation loans, but the problem is much greater than those loans. For example, just last week The Leader-Post of Regina carried a quotation from the Royal Bank of Canada. It reads:
The Royal Bank, one among many, told 84 Saskatchewan farmers last fall that they should get out of business.
"The year before, we didn't tell anyone they should sell out," ... "But it's just not worth it for some of them to put another crop in the ground. The problem is definitely getting larger."
That statement was made by the Royal Bank of Canada. It told farmers: "Quit, before you get too deep into trouble". The quality of farming does not count any more. The best farmers in the area are finding themselves going under because of interest rates. The Farm Credit Corporation could relieve a few of them.
Presently, with capitalization of approximately $132 billion, farmers owe over $20 billion. These are 1982 statistics. That is approximately 15 per cent. That does not sound too bad, but there is a catch because the interest rates are killing the farmers who are trying to start a farming operation. For instance, if a farmer had a $1 million investment in a farm- which these days on the Prairies is a fairly modest farm; a couple of sections of land-and borrowed money at a modest rate of 10 per cent, he would be paying $100,000 interest. In an average year that farmer would be very lucky to make a profit of $80,000 from those two sections of land. If there were no other costs involved, he might be able to meet the interest payments. The only farmers who are able to survive under those circumstances are the farmers who have already capitalized and do not have to depend on the production of their land to keep them going.

Considering all farmers-those who have paid for their land and those who have not paid for their land-of every $2 that they take in income, they pay $1 to the banks and the Farm Credit Corporation for the financing of their operation. What we are recommending is a small relief for that particular problem. We must put the credit on a realistic basis for farmers. We could be very nostalgic about this. A realistic basis for farm credit is approximately 5 per cent. In the days when farmers were able to borrow at 5 per cent, they could make a go of it. As well, the profit margin was greater then. We must put before the agricultural industry some kind of a credit operation which will allow it to farm and continue farming and to finance farming from within the agricultural industry.
In my last few comments I want to put before the House a kind of comprehensive plan for agriculture. In simple terms, which the Government might possibly recognize and understand, we could establish some kind of income stabilization plan which would recognize all of the problems of high input, high taxes, lower returns, high cost of credit and high cost of transportation. Recognizing all of these costs, we could put before the farmers some kind of income stabilization plan so that in the years when things are tough they can survive and in the years they do well, they will possibly make a profit.
If we do that, not necessarily at a rich level but at a secure level, taking into consideration all the factors of production, we can then provide something for the farmers which would keep them going in tough times. I know that some of our friends from the Conservative Party and the Liberal Party may not value the industry enough to try to control the markets in such a way that we are able to do this, but let me say that if the Government cannot bring itself to put forward an income security plan for the farmers, taking into account all these considerations, then we are going to have to do it on a piecemeal basis. And that is really what we are suggesting today.
However, in the long run we really have to go beyond the three suggestions in our motion. Besides providing adequate credit, we must protect the farmers from bankruptcies during the periods they are affected by weather and low prices. We must provide a tax system which would allow a farmer to get started. Right now, it is very difficult for a new farmer to get started because the moment he starts making a littie profit in a good year, he loses it to taxation.
We must establish national marketing agencies which take the speculation and unfairness out of production of some of the crops. We must establish stabilization plans for as many of the products as possible. We must provide low transportation costs and costs of fuel at a level which has some relationship to the price farmers will get for their crops. What we need, Mr. Speaker, is a holistic approach to agricultural problems so that farmers can survive.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a brief comment directed to the previous speaker, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo). I begin by saying I know from previous experience that the Hon. Member's remarks are always well prepared and given very seriously. This was no exception. However, I was attracted to his closing remarks when he used the phrase "an income security plan", and I would like to ask him if he would mind giving us a little more detail. For example, is it a form of stabilization? Is it a plan which the Hon. Member envisages would be based on costs of production for a wide variety of agricultural commodities? Or does he envisage a plan which is more or less on the traditional stop-loss concept based entirely on the market price situation? I feel it would be useful if we had a little more detail.

I see an income stabilization or security plan as one which possibly allows us to dismantle the model situation we presently have which assists the farmer when his apples freeze, but not when he gets hailed out. That is covered by insurance. Right now we have a series of hit and miss stabilization plans, insurance plans and income security plans. Instead of taking each of the crops separately and saying that when you do not make it in this particular crop, your income from your operation, to stay alive, should be within a certain area, I would like to see a method whereby the moment you start hitting that area there is a place where you can go. Perhaps it has to be an insurance plan where you pay in some years and receive in others, such as with the Western Grain Stabilization Plan. Mainly, however, I think we want to put before the farmer some kind of security so that he knows that even when things are bad he is at least going to cover his expenses.
I know there is a problem. U.S. farmers, for example, said, when we were talking about a stable price for grain, well, if we gave $5 a bushel for wheat right across the board they would be ploughing the raspberries under and seeding wheat because there would be some security there. Basing it on price has some dangers. I know from experience that basing it on anything which does not fluctuate to some extent relative to production has some dangers. It is a very complex situation but I think it should be tackled; otherwise we are going to keep on losing farmers at the same rate.

Mr. Speaker, the second part of the Hon. Member's motion refers to:
(2) the repeal of all sales taxes, well-head taxes and other taxes being charged to fuels used for farming and fishing;
I would like to know how many cents per gallon the Hon. Member is talking about there. I would like to know if they have done any research on what the figure is because I have written letters to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres), as well as trying to do some compilations ourselves, and there does not seem to be any hard and fast figure as to how much tax is

actually collected. Can the Hon. Member supply us with any information he might have?
I do not have the figures with me but our understanding is that the total amount collected is something less than $250 million.
For farmers and fishermen?

No, just farmers. For primary industries, I guess we were looking at when we were doing it. Our Party in Saskatchewan did a compilation and came up with seven cents a litre in provincial and federal taxes which could be removed without affecting the amount received by the oil companies. Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a comment and ask the Member a question. I received a letter today from a farmer who felt he just could not make it, so he called an auction sale. He thought he could get enough to satisfy the banks. When the bids came in he got a $3,000 offer for a $50,000 tractor and a $500 offer for a machine worth $75,000. He saw that he was not going to be satisfied that way and had to call off the sale. What he is going to do is sell some of his land from a two-section farm sufficient to satisfy the banks. The farmers are in dire straits and they are now having difficulty keeping their land. Two sections is not very much, and when they have to start selling part of that to satisfy the banks, where are they going to be a year from now? I would like to have the Hon. Member's comments.

I know exactly what the Hon. Member is talking about. The moment they sell that land they reduce their productive base and are less able to pay interest on what they have left. They usually do not reduce their debt, just the interest. Right now in the Western Producer there are ten columns of ads for land for sale, which is about three times as much as there usually is. In my area around Nipawin, Tisdale and Melfort there were over 200 quarters of land available for rent or sale. Farmers are trying to get out now before they have to spend the money to put another crop in the ground. They are farmers, they cannot see the land sit there without producing so they are going to borrow money and put the crop in the ground, but they would rather have someone else do it if possible because they know they are not going to make it. For every farmer who goes bankrupt there are ten who pack up and leave or sell out.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member wonders where the beef is. I know where the baloney is.

I want to say to the Hon. Member who moved the motion today that I visited his area on Sunday evening last and I am fully aware that there are farmers in difficulty. I met about 400 of those farmers in a place called Hudson Bay, a small and fairly nice community of about 2,200. Some of those farmers have not had a crop in three years and they are in a very difficult position, not so much because of what the Government did but because of the weather. Certainly we in the Government have a lot of authority but not enough authority to direct what kind of weather farmers should or should not have. I am sure the Hon. Member is aware of that. He comes across as if it were the Government's fault.
He also talks about the loss of income. World prices of grain have gone down as much as $48 a tonne in less than six months. Is that because of something the Government of Canada did? Our system of supplying the world market with grain through the Canadian Wheat Board is probably one of the most efficient in the world. I am sure the Hon. Member approves of that system. He did not say that, but I have heard him talk about if before. I know his Party stands on that.
He also did not say that there are quite a few farmers in different parts of Canada who do not fit into the bracket he is talking about. Very few of the farmers who have organized themselves into a marketing system and are efficient producers are in economic trouble, unless they did something way outside of normal procedure and good farm management. About 50 per cent of our farmers are still in very good shape in Canada. These are farmers who perhaps did not expand. They are farmers in the kind of productive entities which I mentioned earlier.

The Hon. Member quoted the Catholic Bishops. I would like to quote a priest, Reverend Paul Mooney, who was raised on a farm in Essex County and now lives in Zurich, Ontario where he has a parish. He is quoted in the London Free Press as saying:
Many farmers have gone broke in the last few years. Many got big because the government and banks told them to get big, then everything went haywire. There's been a tremendous human cost in stress and even suicides.
The article goes on:
The greatest enemy is the farmer himself... he's a rugged individualist, Mooney says, not mincing words. I'd hoped the recession had maybe gone deeper so it would get them on their knees and they would do something.
When things are going great farmers are rabid capitalists and free enterprisers for that system. However, when things go bad, even Conservative Members of the House of Commons want the Government to step in and become involved in the free market system. They condemn Crown corporations, but today they are asking us to get more involved in the lending system with the Farm Credit Corporation because the banks refuse to do this for people.
I am pleased that the Members opposite have given us the opportunity to debate this important subject. I am glad that they share my concern for farmers and my enthusiasm about the potential for the industry as well. The motion asks that the House recognize the tremendous financial difficulty that farmers have been placed under. That is something which Members on this side of the House have recognized for a long time, Mr. Speaker. We have gone beyond recognition to action. We have undertaken a whole series of initiatives to help farmers deal with the pressures of a difficult economic time.
I can list a host of programs which the Government has initiated. It has initiated advance payments for stored crops, stabilization plans, support for fruit and vegetable storage construction, shared cost programs with the provinces for agricultural development, special interest rates for farmers in financial difficulty, and enabling legislation for national marketing programs. The list goes on and on, Mr. Speaker. Hon. Members talk as though the Government had done nothing.
The Hon. Member who tabled this motion comes from the Province of Saskatchewan where agriculture is the basic and most important industry. What have their previous NDP and present Conservative Governments done with agriculture? They have done very little compared with what the federal Government does. In Saskatchewan the federal Government spends practically double what either the previous or present governments have. We also provide the benefit of the Farm Credit Corporation and advance interest-free loans on crops. The total involvement of the federal Government in Saskatchewan is nearly $500 million a year, whereas the province contributes less than $100 million a year.
The Hudson Bay district is called a disaster area. However, the Premier of Saskatchewan has never officially written a letter to me, to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or anyone else saying that it is a disaster area and they would like the Government to participate in the program. They have told me they are going to put money in their budget for this and want

the federal Government to participate. I told them we would listen to their representation as soon as it was made. However, up until yesterday we had not received such a letter. The Government of Saskatchewan brought its budget in several weeks ago and has never made that official request. That government allocated $4 million in its budget and suggested the federal Government match that. However, that request has never been officially made in writing although the Minister of Agriculture and Premier of Saskatchewan know the proper procedures.
The motion mentions three specific things and I will try to deal with them in order. The suggestion that the federal Government issue an interim payment from the Western Grain Stabilization Fund is very tempting, Mr. Speaker, to say the least. There is no doubt that many western grain farmers are experiencing financial difficulty. That is why we have taken the initiative to amend the Act so that the payments will be based on a crop year rather than a calendar year and that the triggering mechanism will be changed to take into account per unit cash flow as well as total income.
As I said in Winnipeg last week, the Western Grain Stabilization Act is the main federal program protecting incomes of prairie grain farmers. It is a voluntary Act, Mr. Speaker. Farmers may join it if they want to. About 75 per cent of the grain farmers joined it and 25 per cent have not seen fit to join. Through that program the federal Government contributes $2 for every $1 contributed by the farmers. We administer the Act and pay interest on the total accumulation of funds every year.
It is like a black hole. All the money goes in and nothing comes out.

The basic concept of the program is very sound, but we need to change the pay-out mechanism to provide a more stable level of support, especially during prolonged periods of depressed world prices and markets. World prices and world markets have a greater effect on farmers' incomes than anything else, and they know it.
On the surface it would seem that to make an interim payment would be an easy thing to do. Let us first look at some practical considerations. When we made interim payments in the past it was after the end of the year under review and because we knew the receipts had projections of costs. With all this data the existing formula indicated that a payment was going to be required. That formula today does not indicate a payment will be required for 1983. There is no way the present legislation can trigger a payment. That is precisely why, on April 25, the Government announced that legislation would be introduced to amend the Western Grain Stabilization Act. We are planning to improve the program and expect that these improvements will trigger a substantial pay-out to producers for 1983-84. I expect the Western Grain Stabilization Act to be introduced within a matter of a few days.
Earlier I indicated that we were considering the possibility of making an interim payment after the Bill had received

Let us take another look at the question of making an interim payment. We must first remember that a major thrust of this legislation is to make payments more promptly. The proposed switch to a crop year instead of a calendar year means that a farmer would only have to wait until October or November, just two or three months following the end of the crop year, for a payment. Under the existing Act, Mr. Speaker, there is a delay of nearly 10 months from the end of the calendar year until payments can be processed. The legislation does not allow any triggering. Last year 37 million tonnes of grain were sold, the largest volume in Canada's history. We do not have the time to study the formula here, but the western grain stabilization people in Winnipeg will show you exactly what triggers the plan.
That has nothing to do with it.

It does not trigger under that volume system. However, by greatly reducing the length of time between the end of the crop year and a possible pay-out, the new legislation should correspondingly reduce the need for interim payments.

There would also be substantial administrative problems to overcome if we were to make an interim payment under the new legislation. The thing is that expenses considered under this program are calculated by Statistics Canada using a July 1 reference date, and it takes a couple of months after that to produce the final figures. It would be difficult to project those figures in the absence of the survey data.
It is also difficult to project receipts. What about when you run into unforeseen problems such as what happened when the St. Clair River was plugged full of ice? The boats could not move and millions of dollars were lost every day. That situation had never taken place in the Great Lakes since shipping was started in the Great Lakes system. There were over 100 boats held up. At least 50 per cent of those boats, I would think, were boats coming from the Lakehead or boats going up to the Lakehead load up with grain. That cost millions and millions of dollars and there was a backlog of hundreds of thousands of cars of grain sitting on sidings because the elevators in the Thunder Bay area were chock full of grain. Everything was supposed to go according to schedule, but it did not go according to schedule because of the ice phenomenon that took place in Lake Huron and in the St. Clair River.
Finally it must be noted that if the legislation is passed, we will likely be making a payment of roughly $300 million in late October. I would argue that prairie farmers will need that money just as much in the fall as in the spring. Many farmers operate on a line of credit. They borrow in the spring and repay the money in the fall. Farmers also make a lot of their machinery purchases in the fall. Land payments are usually made in the fall also.

Mir. Whelan: Federal taxes on fuel are made up, as the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson) mentioned, of 1.5 cents per litre excise tax on gasoline and a 9 per cent sales tax on gasoline and diesel fuel. The 1.5 cents per litre excise tax is rebated to all commercial users, including farmers. And there is no excise tax on diesel oil or propane.
Exemption from the sales tax on fuels used by farmers would save Canadian farmers an estimated $91 million a year. The Government, however, would not only lose that $91 million in revenue, but it would have to set up a complex and expensive mechanism for policing such a rebate.
In the past decade, a major consideration in government policy has been to maintain a close relationship in farm fuel costs with the United States. Fuel price monitoring by the Government has shown that between 1976 and 1978, the U.S. enjoyed a small advantage of one to two cents per litre over Canadian retail fuel prices. The advantage turned in Canada's favour by 4.5 to six cents per litre during 1971-1981, even though taxes in Canada remained two to four cents a litre higher than in the U.S.A.
That is ancient history. This is not a history course.

During this period, prices in both Canada and the U.S. remained substantially lower than in the European Economic Community countries, such as the United Kingdom, France, Italy and West Germany, again countries with which we compete.
In the last couple of years, we have witnessed a very substantial rationalization in the Canadian petroleum refining sector. This is partly due to the deep recession we have been through, and partly due to the successful conservation efforts by all sectors in Canada. Rationalization has brought with it retail price wars which have benefited all consumers, including farmers.
The Government is always willing to discuss ways in which input costs to food production can be reduced. As you know, a Private Member's motion is presently before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance, Trade, and Economic Affairs. Debate on this subject will provide ample opportunity to review farm fuel taxes in relation to other sectors.

I would first like to point out that the FCC has loans outstanding to 79,000 farmers. The recent increase in interest rates is of concern to all Canadians. Like other Canadians, farmers will undoubtedly alter investment and borrowing plans because of changes in interest rates. You are all aware of the Small Business Development Bond Program under which a total of 17,263 loans were made for $2.7 billion to December 31, 1981. Of this amount, 2,902 loans for $587 million were extended to farmers and fishermen. On December 31, 1981 the program changed to the Small Business Bond and has been used for debt consolidation purposes. Since January 1, 1982 a total of 2,878 loans for $562 million have been approved to farmers.
This program in collaboration with commercial lenders provides credit at interest rates substantially below the current market rate, about half the regular cost of borrowing money. When the interest rate was 20 per cent, farmers could borrow under that program at 11 per cent, and a lot of them did.
The Farm Credit Corporation has been a major force in providing credit to the farm sector under reasonable terms and conditions. In the fiscal year that just ended on March 31, 1984, the Farm Credit Corporation extended 5,736 loans for about $758 million, the largest level of lending activity in its history. These funds were extended at interest rates of between 12.75 and 13.5 per cent. Of all the loans extended, 962 loans for $175 million were extended under the Special Farm Financial Assistance Program where farmers receive a four percentage point rebate for two years. Mr. Speaker, I have been listening to a very interesting discussion between Members of the Official Opposition and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). I would now like to take this opportunity to speak to the motion before the House today, a motion that very accurately reflects the recommendations my party has been making to the Government, especially in the past two years. We are stressing the importance of making a substantial payment from the Western Grain Stabilization Fund to assist with seeding costs; the need for repealing all sales taxes to help farmers; and the need for an immediate interest rate reduction on Farm Credit Corporation loans. These are some very pertinent recommendations the Progressive Conservative Party has been making and has been urging the Government, whose insensitivity is almost obscene, to implement.
Mr. Speaker, before going any further with my comments I would like to remind the House that I knew the Minister of Agriculture when he was a member of the Standing Committee on Agriculture. I remember very clearly how he insisted on the importance of long term agricultural policies and how at every meeting, he would emphasize the need for security and stability in the agricultural industry. I must say that, as Minister of Agriculture, he has not succeeded in practicing what he preached as a member of the committee. Maybe it was easier at the time for him to say what he wanted and what he wanted his Government to do, but as Minister, he has not succeeded in giving this vital sector of our economy the stability and security he was seeking at the time. Of course, the Minister never misses an opportunity to point out what he has accomplished. Mr. Speaker, I admit there are sectors that are doing fairly well, and I am thinking of dairy farmers. It is a fact that there has been a very substantial improvement, and my comments in this respect must be positive. Where the agricultural industry as a whole has a turnover of $50 billion, the dairy sector's share is $18 billion. As I said, agriculture generates a turnover of $50 billion, and affects about one-fifth of the labour force. Considering that agriculture is a very special industry, as the Minister is no doubt aware, I would have expected him to explain how the agricultural industry differs from industry in general. If we agree, Mr. Speaker, that we have to eat in order to live, and not the other way around, we must be consistent when dealing with an industry like agriculture. We must explain with all due honesty, to all Canadians and Canadian business people, that the agricultural industry pursues that objective and that its needs are so special that we cannot make an economic assessment of agriculture as we would of any other industry. We must ensure the survival of agriculture and we must continue to promote agriculture, for the well-being of our fellow citizens. And if we are consistent, if we believe in this principle, we must propose and introduce legislation that is finely tuned to the needs of an industry that is vitally important to our economic development

and to the Canadian economy. However, it has a very special mission, one that is very relevant to our responsibilities as Members of this House. Mr. Speaker, the Minister is going to say once again that he has spent millions and millions and millions of dollars which, in some cases were wasted through lack of planning. That is what we have against the Department of Agriculture and this Government, Mr. Speaker.
We would like to see an agricultural policy based on the principle that we must feed Canadians, and that we must do so without political interference. Ensuring that Canadians have access to high quality food is certainly a praiseworthy goal which we should be defending here in the House, and if that is true and if all Members of this House shared this view, Hon. Members would have no trouble rising above partisan considerations and establishing long term policies, instead of merely seeking payments just before an election. Mr. Speaker, I think the time has come to ask the Government, and 1 may point out that what I am saying in the House today arises from profound convictions and a very special concern that I have, first of all, for the farmers in my constituency and also for farmers in the West, the East and Ontario. We have to make sure that our agricultural policy is impartial. That is important. Bearing in mind the principles we are called upon to uphold in this House and our own responsibilities, we should be able to meet as often as necessary with the provinces, the agricultural sector and the farming communities involved so as to establish a truly long-term agricultural policy which puts the emphasis on both stability and profitability. Such is the

May 3, 1984
Supply
role and responsibility of a Minister of Agriculture and a Government whose primary concern should be to see to it that people have enough to eat. By the same token, we Canadians as a country might be still more generous than we have been so far with respect to the Third World and other nations where people are actually starving to death.
Our agricultural capacity is potentially unlimited and our climate enables us to initiate rather extraordinary endeavours. The technology is there, Mr. Speaker, but financing does seem to be a problem. Because he was unable to come up with adequate policies in hard times, the Minister must be held responsible for his failure to look far enough into the future to realize that our economic situation might worsen, as numerous precedents have shown. Precisely because it was unable to see what the future had in store for us, we are quite justified in censuring the Government for such unforgiveable oversights which have put thousands of farmers in a precarious situation, even though the Government is not doing anything to help them out of their predicament. Why did this Government in particular wait until it was confronted with urgent problems, instead of making concerted efforts with the provinces and the people directly concerned in an attempt to face up to the situation and find policies designed to restore stability? Nothing has been done. The Government chose to take a band-aid approach every time a group of farmers or agricultural communities from Eastern or Western Canada sought assistance. As a result of such undependable policies, thousands of farmers have been forced right out of the agricultural sector in the past few years.
Mr. Speaker, I too represent a province where agriculture is a significant economic component. But again I must say that if we fail to keep in mind the basic principle that a Government must first make sure that the people have enough food on the table, all our arguments rest on meaningless premises, we are going the wrong way and we are not facing up to our responsibilities. I would go even further, Mr. Speaker, and suggest that all Members should realize that the agricultural context has changed so much that it is no longer possible to run farming operations the way it was done before. We are all aware of that and we know that family farms are not passed on from fathers to sons, but that they can be sold and bought. We know how much money is involved and we realize that young farmers today must carry enormous debts. We all know that, Mr. Speaker, yet nothing has been done to find a solution. We readily lend money to a farmer, but we are not quite so eager to sit down with him and help him get through hard times when he is experiencing difficulties with his operations. We are aware of that. Perhaps $15,000 or $20,000 would do nicely 25, 30 or 40 years ago, but these days we are talking in terms of $300,000 and $400,000.
The son of a farmer who owned his land can go into debt because the possibilities are there. There are tools, farm credit
is available, so he can apply for a loan. The problem is that he cannot make ends meet as a result of past and current interest rates. The farmer cannot meet his financial obligations and at the same time run a profitable operation to ensure his future on the farm. We are aware of that, but we have yet to take appropriate action. We shall have to consider developing policies to help the young farmer who wants to buy a $300,000 farm, because the Minister knows as well as I do that, with today's interest rates, and I am not saying that he is responsible for them, we cannot meet this need for continuity in family farms and the farming industry. We know about this and we have to be ready in the near future to examine with complete objectivity how and through which policies we can prepare and guarantee this takeover of the industry by younger farmers. As I said earlier, we have a basic responsibility to ensure the survival of the farming industry and this cannot be achieved without stability and security. Therefore, we must think it over seriously and develop policies designed to give the young farmers who are only too willing to continue in agriculture the financial means to purchase their parents' farms and this does not mean what it did 35, 40 or 50 years ago. It seems to me that this Government has yet to understand this situation which is still quite new but which now exists and will continue to exist.
In the circumstances, we clearly cannot be satisfied with a Minister of Agriculture telling us what he has done, the efforts he has made and the millions he has spent, wasted or handed out. Of course, the Government has done certain things, but it was always to solve a problem which was already something of the past, when the harm had already been done. This is a piecemeal approach, Mr. Speaker, and not a long term policy. I therefore urge the Minister of Agriculture today to think seriously of the co-operation which he should promote instead of fanning competition with the Provinces as is now the case. What I want to hear, Mr. Speaker, is not that the Minister has given more to the Quebec Government or that Mr. Garon should have invested in Quebec's agricultural industry. What I want to hear is that the Federal Minister is willing to discuss, negotiate and find a solution about marketing boards, for instance, especially as concerns the joint pork plan. What I want to hear, Mr. Speaker, is that something has been done to compensate for the weather problem last summer in the Province of Quebec, and probably elsewhere. In any case, I have received representations telling me that the farmers lost millions of dollars. This was not easy to accept in view of the increase in interest rates, but the farmers have pulled through. A request has also been made to the Quebec Government, and it seems that the Federal Government is waiting to see how Quebec will respond. I urge the Minister of Agriculture on behalf of thousands of Quebec producers to call a meeting if need be. If there is any lack of good faith on the part of his Quebec counterpart, I urge the Minister of Agriculture to organize the meeting by himself in the interests of the farmers. It does not matter to me whether the Federal Minister of
May 3, 1984

Agriculture likes or dislikes his counterpart in Quebec, Saskatchewan or any other Province. What is important is that the Federal Minister of Agriculture should know that he has a duty to the farmers and the Canadian population to ensure the survival of our agriculture. Mr. Speaker, that is why I would like to see policies based on an objective approach that would rise above partisan considerations which certainly do not have their place in an area as vital as the future and survival of agriculture.
Mr. Speaker, that is what I had to say, and I did not want to spend my time criticizing the Minister of Agriculture but rather, I want to ask him to start concentrating now on the survival of the agricultural industry and the policies that will ensure its continuation, policies that should be developed in co-operation with all sectors concerned and with the provinces. Mr. Speaker, I appeal today to the Minister of Agriculture, in the spirit of true federalism, and I would do so to any Minister of Agriculture, to bear in mind the concerns of our farmers. Many other sectors are equally concerned about economic policies that have failed to achieve the results promised by this Government and anxiously awaited by all Canadians. Once again, the Minister must realize that agriculture is a vital industry, that it is not like any other industry in this country, and that there is one objective, one goal we must all strive for, which is to give Canadians access to quality food at a reasonable price.
We must be prepared to act responsibly and realize that this industry is very special and requires special measures which we have a duty to take and are expected to take by the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions or comments?

Mr. Speaker, I would just like to ask the Hon. Member if he is aware of what is going on. It sounds as if we treat provinces differently. Quebec does not receive treatment different from any other province. It has refused to sign the agreement on crop insurance. Every other province has agreed to it.
Does he also not realize that almost 50 per cent of the farm income in Quebec is from the dairy industry? Does he not realize that the industry really started to become healthy from November, 1972? Does he also not realize that on the matter of frozen apple trees the federal Government moved in, not only in Quebec but in Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, because they had a variety of trees which were uninsurable, and it cost us over a period of two years about $56 million?
He intimates there is confrontation. Quebec producers have made representations to me about crop losses. Under the agreement we have with all the provinces, if the province feels the loss is too big for them, then they make representations to the federal Government. I have not received that kind of
Supply
representation from the Province of Quebec. They have said they will participate in the plan but they have not made that kind of official representation to the federal Government. I take it for granted that it is the provincial government which refused to do that because the last time I met with the provincial minister in Ottawa we talked about a stabilization program for pork and he seemed to be very agreeable at that time. I do not know what his position is at present. I know, Mr. Speaker, that you are very much aware of the fact that we do not have a potato marketing agency for eastern Canada because Quebec, not the producers but the province, has refused to go ahead with that. Is the Hon. Member suggesting that I take over total authority for agriculture? I do not know for sure but under the Constitution I probably could.

Mr. Speaker, first of all to answer the Minister's question I would like to point out that I did not accuse the Minister of any lack of co-operation or objectivity in his dealings which the Government of the Province of Quebec. I did not accuse the Minister of being less than honest with the Government of Quebec. I merely said, Mr. Speaker, that assuming that at some time, certain provincial ministers ... I remember hearing about losses incurred as a result of weather conditions last summer. When the Minister of Agriculture is prepared to make a recommendation, I will also be prepared to consider it. Obviously, it is always the same old story: Is it the province or the federal Government? I am simply asking the Minister, in view of his responsibilities, to make his position clear. While the Minister cannot be blamed if a provincial minister turns down a generous offer or ignores a positive response from the federal Government, on the other hand, we ought to know exactly what the federal Minister is prepared to do about a given request, depending on the situation. In any case, I suggest, and this is not meant as criticism, I suggest and I recommend increased co-operation for the purpose of establishing a national agricultural policy, corresponding to the needs of all sectors and all regions.
I feel the principle of decentralization with respect to farm products and agricultural sectors should be seen within the context of a broad national policy. I would especially urge the Minister to show even greater willingness to co-operate and to consult with the sectors concerned.
Mr. Speaker, does the Hon. Member not realize that I am probably the most approachable and co-operative Minister of Agriculture on the Federal and provincial scene?

Mr. Speaker, I am not saying that the Minister does not know how to co-operate, but when I see how important the agricultural sector is and when I see the need for setting up agricultural policies that should rise above partisan consideration, and I assume the Minister agrees with me, I

May 3, 1984
Supply
want to ask the Minister to set up agricultural policies that are not subject to political pressures and especially not introduced the day before an election.

Mr. Speaker, has the Hon. Member not studied the agri-food strategy which developed after 180-odd meetings across Canada? In my view and that of many other people, this is the most advanced 20-year agricultural program of any country in the world.

Mr. Speaker, I repeat what I said before, and I do so willingly, because I think it cannot be said often enough. What is important in Parliament, as the Minister is aware, is that we can use a motion to demand immediate proposals. We regret the delay with respect to measures that must be taken to cope with the problems facing farmers today. I also urge the Minister, speaking on behalf of millions of farmers, to show greater willingness to consult and hold meetings with the sectors concerned in order to develop policies that will provide security for farmers, which is what we are seeking, and especially stability and the assurance that their farms will survive, which is far from certain today, considering the economic situation. That is all we want.

subsubtopic: PLEA ON BEHALF OF UNBORN CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every Hon. Member of the House, along with thoudands of Canadians, has grieved with the parents of the babies murdered in the Toronto Children's Hospital, as the stories on the Grange Commission's inquiry appeared in front page news throughout Canada. How could anyone kill such innocent and helpless babies?
Yet every week across this nation, not only in Toronto but in every major city in the country, helpless unborn babies are being aborted, and the daily press scarcely mentions these murders. More space is given to the hue and cry when baby seals are killed than when these helpless human beings are denied life. It is ironic that there is so much interest in trying to find the person responsible for the terrible deaths in Toronto, while at the same time many in our society condone or say nothing about respected doctors and hospitals in their own communities removing unborn children, human beings, from the wombs of their mothers.
When are the Government and the House of Commons going to show concern for unborn babies equal to that which they show when a born baby is killed? Neither should be accepted, and yet taxpayers' money is now being used to encourage abortion, not to save the life of the mother or of the child, but as a birth control measure. These innocent and helpless babies, born and unborn, are created by an omnipotent God. How long is Government going to condemn one and condone the other?

Mr. Speaker, CP is showing substantial profits, especially on its railroading-no pun intended. In fact, The Globe and Mail reports this morning that CP is "heading for a speedy recovery". Western farmers should also be aware that at a time when they are experiencing record financial problems the CPR is making good profits, and that John Turner has just been re-appointed to its board of directors.
That is typical of the Government, Mr. Speaker, because it has a miserable record as far as Canadian agriculture is concerned. In fact there is only one bill on the Order Paper in this session pertaining to agriculture. That is Bill C-23, a Bill to increase cash advances on prairie grain. This morning in the House the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) berated the Opposition for holding up this Bill. In fact, the opposite is true. We on this side have supported the Minister and promised quick passage of the Bill, but even our support does not appear
May 3, 1984

to be enough for the Minister, because the Government House Leader (Mr. Pinard) has not even called the Bill for second reading yet.
The same is true for two other measures the Government is apparently proposing; a red meat stabilization plan, and amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Act. The Government has asked us for support, but surely we cannot be expected to support phantom Bills. We must see the Bills before we can support them, the only thing that has been passed in this session pertaining to Canadian agriculture has come from this side. The Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) had a motion passed referring the Agri-bond concept to the finance committee. The Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) also had a motion passed asking for a reduction in federal taxes on fuels used in farming and fishing.
We on this side are serious about assisting producers of food. The Government, unfortunately, is only interested in putting the blame on someone else for its own inadequacies.
The Hon. Member's time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment on de Havilland in Toronto and the latest leaked report about the difficulties of that Crown corporation. I put a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) some time ago, and he turned it back on me saying that it was a question of either jobs or cash-we had to give the cash to keep the jobs and, if we did not give the cash we would not get the jobs. Well, we have given the cash, and now we are going to have cutbacks in the jobs. That is an untenable situation.
I checked with the people on the shop floor of de Havilland this morning. I found that de Havilland has top heavy management. For example, in 1981 there were 3,500 employees on the shop floor and 1,900 management employees. In 1984 there are 1,300 floor employees and 1,400 management employees. I found out that there is a slush fund for management retirees, and nothing for the workers except further lay-offs.
On behalf of the NDP I would like to suggest four things. One, we must support this industry. I remember, from my childhood in Etobicoke, the difficulties AV Roe had when the Avro-Arrow was cancelled. We must support our aeronautics industry. Second, we must support export credits, as other countries are doing that. Third, we must have some new initiatives. We must update. We should be flying to Ottawa in Dash-8s rather than DC-9s, for short hauls. Fourth, we must have accountability. We must have a corporate plan ratified by Parliament.
The Hon. Member's time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, for the third time I rise in the House to deal with the injustice which is being perpetrated on gratuity income earners throughout Canada and which the Minister responsible at the federal level has not deemed advisable to rectify by making it possible for them to get benefits consistent with their global incomes. Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, you will realize why, on behalf of the 60,000 gratuity income earners in Quebec alone, I must beseech and beg the government to introduce the necessary amendment as soon as possible, so that these workers who must bear the brunt of these hard times may be eligible to unemployment insurance benefits consistent with their incomes.
Mr. Speaker, 1 dare hope, that the six dozens of Hon. Members from Quebec who certainly realize the importance of my motion, will not hesitate to twist the arm of the Minister responsible to settle this matter before it is too late.
The reason I had to rise in the House today to deal again with this issue is that so far I have received no reply from my hon. friends opposite.

subtopic: SCHEDULED VISIT OF HER MAJESTY-OPPOSITION TO POSSIBLE CANCELLATION
SCHEDULED VISIT OF HER MAJESTY-OPPOSITION TO POSSIBLE CANCELLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1984 marks the date for two significant anniversaries in the life of our nation. The visit to Canada of our country's head of state, Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, is a fitting tribute to celebrate 200 years as a province in New Brunswick, and the bicentennial of the arrival of the United Empire Loyalists in Ontario.
As Head of State, Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth is an important part of our Canadian heritage.
The Queen's visit will promote enthusiasm and interest in those areas where she will be present, and will provide local tourism with a much needed stimulus, particularly as unemployment remains a problem in Canada.
A decision to cancel the visit of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II for a summer election would be viewed by Canadians with considerable regret. The suggestion in today's edition of The Citizen by a Liberal source, which reads: "Those who would be really upset by the cancellation of the Royal visit don't vote for us anyway", should read: "All Canadians regardless of political stripe won't vote Liberal if a cancellation occurs for partisan political reasons."

May 3, 1984
As our national Head of State, the Queen is above partisan politics. I invite government Members to consider the seriousness of this irresponsible newspaper quote before any hasty decision is made to cancel the Queen's visit for any reason.

Prairie farmers are now getting the opportunity to see first hand the effects of the new Crow rate regime at their local elevator. Freight charges are to go up a whopping $1.90 a tonne, or an increase of 35 per cent on August 1 this year on average, with increases of up to 45 per cent for farmers in Manitoba. This comes at a time when farm bankruptcies have gone up by 78 per cent on the Prairies over the same period last year and grain prices are falling.
Farmers were worried about the cap on federal contributions, and we in the New Democratic Party tried to have this cap removed. Now, because farmers have moved a larger volume of grain in an attempt to pay their bills, they are being penalized with an average increase of 35 per cent in their freight rate even though actual costs for the railroad have risen only 4 per cent in the same period.
Government advertisements last year said rates would increase "gradually from the current 13 cents per bushel to about 25 cents in four years". Actually on average farmers have had to pay an extra 1.5 cents per bushel from January 1, 1984, and now with an additional 5 cents per bushel on August 1, 1984 this amounts to an increase of 6.5 cents per bushel in just seven months. So much for government promises compared with government actions.

Mr. Speaker, approximately two years ago the bells rang in this House continuously for almost two weeks. The work of the House stalled, the Official Opposition went on strike, with cause. I was concerned. I wrote to then Speaker Madame Sauve on March 9, 1982, and I said:
Without firm and direct action by the Speaker to resolve this question, a dangerous precedent will be established for the future-one that will allow Opposition Parties to abruptly halt the work of Parliament at will and for indefinite periods of time.
Yes, the precedent set by this Parliament has spread. The ringing of the bells was used in the Manitoba Legislature, resulting in adjournment of its session. Then it was used in Saskatchewan by the Official Opposition. It will spread to other legislatures. In the Alberta Legislature, the Official Opposition consists of two NDP Members. Are they to be
permitted to shut down the Alberta Legislature at will by a bell-ring episode?
The Canadian people are just beginning to realize the enormity and the consequences of the use of this unusual procedure to halt the nation's business. I believe that a constitutional amendment is necessary to place bounds on this growing cancer. To stimulate discussion on the matter, it is my intention to bring forth a Private Member's Bill incorporating a constitutional amendment to limit and place bounds on this growing disruptive parliamentary practice.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN BANK OF CANADA RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister, and of the Minister of Finance on the day the Bank of Canada rate comes out, it is difficult to know to whom to address a question. I will ask the Acting Prime Minister, if there is one. There are seven of them out in the country acting now as though they would like to be Prime Minister.
The Bank of Canada rate has just gone up again to 11.13 per cent, a considerable increase, which means that bank prime interest rates and all interest rates will be going up. Interest rates have gone up over 2 per cent on 365-day bills since the Budget was brought down. The Canadian dollar has decreased in value something like 3 cents since the Budget was brought down. Our gross domestic product is going down and not up, and the country is in a desperate economic shape. Will the Government now bring in new policies or a new Budget, or take some action that will start to reverse these horrendous economic developments since the Budget of February 15?

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN BANK OF CANADA RATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member opposite is being his usual exaggerated self when he speaks of the economy being in-what was his word-horrendous shape. Of course the economy is not in horrendous shape. The economy is in very good shape, and it is getting better all the time.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN BANK OF CANADA RATE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speechtext:
If the Member opposite had any ability to understand economic facts he would know perfectly well that the growth in the economy is proceeding at a stable and effective rate. We are seeing improvements in the manufacturing industry. Interest rates and unemployment are not increasing at any level which should cause real hardship or real concern today.
When the Hon. Member opposite speaks of the impact of interest rates in the economy, he should realize that the
May 3, 1984

increases have been of a minimal nature. They are not of a substantial character. They arise in part, as he knows perfectly well, from interest rate increases in the United States. Over the longer run the circumstances of the Canadian economy will ensure that those interest rate increases are not of a massive nature.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see the Minister of Finance has come into the House. I want to ask him about interest rates. As he no doubt knows, the Bank of Canada rate has just gone up to 11.13 per cent. The Minister of Finance heard the halting and unintelligible answer of the Minister of State for Finance when I asked him my question.
The Minister of Finance said on March 22, 1984:
Our policy is to keep interest rates as low as we can sensibly keep them in this country and still have an economy which will grow.
In view of the fact that interest rates are now going up again and the economy is not growing, will the Minister take action to reverse this state of affairs? Will he admit that his February 15 Budget was of no assistance, and will he now take other actions and bring in other measures before this House to try to reverse the terrible position in which we now find ourselves?
Mr. Speaker, First I heard not an unintelligible but a very intelligent answer from the Minister of State for Finance.
Hear, hear!
We didn't.

If it was unintelligible, the problem is with the Hon. Member who asked the question, not with the person who gave the answer.
As far as interest rates are concerned, indeed the bank rate went up today by 0.29 per cent of a point. That follows a situation where we have upward pressure in the United States, as the Hon. Member knows, but even at the present moment the prime rate at the banks, which is the rate that affects people most, is still half a point below that in the United States. My hon. friend knows that.
As far as the economy not growing is concerned, my friend is wrong again. The Canadian economy is growing, and it is growing at a rate that compares favourably with most other industrial economies at the present time.
As far as the request which the Hon. Member has put forward is concerned, I have indicated that the Budget of February 15 contained a number of measures, and some of them are already before the House. I hope they will get quick and early consideration by the House. I was disappointed to see that some measures that would have helped business, in spite of an agreement with some spokesmen for the Conservative Party, have not received the early consideration that we were promised. I hope we will be receiving quick and early
Oral Questions
consideration of those measures because they will be beneficial to the taxpayers of this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my final supplementary is directed to the Minister of Finance. The Minister's policies have had a singular lack of success. In the United States there is growth of over 8 per cent this quarter, whereas in Canada we are having a decline, not growth.
The Minister said in the House on March 26 that he was monitoring the situation carefully. Everything that has happened since March 26 has been bad. He went on to say:
If need be, we will make the necessary adjustments. In the meantime I see no reason to change the basic policy that we have been following.
Since then the unemployment rate is up again, and over 1.5 million Canadians are out of work, interest rates are up, and the dollar is down. When will the Minister show some concern? When will he listen to Canadians and take some steps to try to relieve the situation in which we find ourselves? The answers he has given in the House are unsupportable, unsavory, and unsatisfactory. When will he take some steps to adjust the situation in accordance with these facts which today show that interest rates will go up again?

Mr. Speaker, 1 was ready to welcome the Hon. Member back to the House because he has been away for quite some time, but I did not know that he had been outside the country as well. Indeed, he will be happy to hear that, contrary to what he said, the Canadian economy in the first quarter did not decline. It has increased. It may not have increased as much as the Hon. Member would have preferred, but it has increased.
What did it do in February?
What he says is completely wrong and false, and the rest of his question follows on that false premise.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO DISBAND THREE GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
PROPOSAL TO DISBAND THREE GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Finance. speechtext: Quite obviously, Mr. Speaker, that is the kind of question which should not be directed to me, but perhaps I might give the same answer as the one I gave to the previous question and say that at least the Liberal Party has people who think about the future.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ORDER BANK RATE ROLLED BACK
REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ORDER BANK RATE ROLLED BACK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. It concerns the increase in interest rates. He has just suggested to the House, in his smiling way, that the increase is not really that great. He will now know that the rate is at its highest level in 18 months. Also he will know that we have had a record number of small business bankruptcies in the past two years, that farm bankruptcies are increasing this year at a rate, depending upon the province, of 100 per cent to 150 per cent or 160 per cent, and that all businessmen across Canada are saying that, if we do not have lower interest rates, whatever recovery we now have may be stopped.
Considering that the Liberals promised in the 1980 election campaign to have a made-in-Canada low interest rate policy, will he deliver what they promised and order Governor Bouey
to roll back the interest rate increase which was announced today?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ORDER BANK RATE ROLLED BACK
speechtext:

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGE IN METHOD OF ESTABLISHING BANK RATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. The Minister has been blaming American interest rates for our problems. Will he at least do one thing to establish confidence in the country? Will he change the method by which the Bank of Canada rate is established? Will he direct the rate at which the Bank of Canada will advance money to the chartered banks in a way that is consistent with keeping jobs in the Canadian economy and building the economy, instead of having our whole interest rate structure depend on a daily or weekly option of Treasury bills?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGE IN METHOD OF ESTABLISHING BANK RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the commercial Canadian bank rates are not purely determined by the weekly auction by the Bank of Canada. The best evidence of this is that the Bank of Canada rate has moved up over the last several weeks without a similar increase in the prime rate by the commercial banks. There is no automatic relationship between what happens with the Bank of Canada rate and the commercial rates that are available to Canadians from the commercial banks.
If my friend looks at the daily comparison of selected Canadian and U.S. yields, for example, he will find that on 30-day prime corporate paper, in March and April the Canadian rate has been lower than the American rate, not higher, and that the 90-day prime corporate rate has been very lightly over the American rate. In fact the latest figure I have is at the same level as in the United States. I do not think my friend can argue seriously that Canadian rates are systematically higher than American rates. Evidence in the last several weeks has been to the contrary.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Hovdebo:
That this House recognizes the tremendous financial difficulty that farmers have been placed under and therefore recommends that the government immediately consider injection of much needed cash into farming through:
(1)	the immediate payout of a substantial initial payment from the Western
Grain Stabilization Fund in order to assist with seeding costs;
(2)	the repeal of all sales taxes, well-head taxes and other taxes being
charged to fuels used for farming and fishing; and
(3)	an immediate interest rate reduction on Farm Credit Corporation loans
