subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to speak on this particular Opposition motion put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), that this House recognizes the tremendous financial difficulty that farmers have been placed under and therefore recommends that the Government immediately consider injection of much needed cash into farming through the three points mentioned here: the immediate pay-out of a substantial initial payment from the Western Grain Stabilization Fund in order to assist with seeding costs; the repeal of all sales taxes, well-head taxes and other taxes being charged to fuels used for farming and fishing; and an immediate interest rate reduction on Farm Credit Corporation loans so that viable refinancing of farms can take place.
This particular motion is threefold and focuses on things that have been emphasized in the House over the last little while. It focuses on the Western Grain Stabilization Fund, the question of sales and well-head taxes charged for fuels, and the question of Farm Credit Corporation loans in order that farmers who are refinancing their loans at this time would be able to refinance at a reasonable rate.
I have received letters on all of these issues from farmers in my constituency, Mr. Speaker. All of them have been requesting action on each of the points mentioned above. Regarding the Western Grain Stabilization Plan, a farmer from Sifton in my riding writes:
I feel that the formula should be re-written to tie in the cost of production along with returns for production, i.e. net returns as opposed to gross returns.
Grain has not changed drastically, however, cost of production has skyrocketted, thereby placing extreme burdens on farmers.
The letter from this farmer in Sifton continues:
Perhaps Eugene Whelan would be willing to re-examine the present formula in view of the fact that he is considering running as leader of the federal Liberals and he needs western support.
This need for an immediate pay-out is something which all of us in the New Democratic Party have been raising. I was glancing at the statement I made on March 5 in the House which pointed out the fact that the projected net farm income
in Manitoba for 1984 is lower than the actual net income in 1973. Before the Easter break we offered the Minister all the co-operation of the New Democratic Party to have these amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Act passed but nothing happened. We had the announcement during the Easter break and still nothing happened. On April 30 we were here, Mr. Speaker, and nothing happened. May 1 came around and nothing happened. May 2 came around and nothing happened. Today is May 3 and the Minister appears to have been talking through his invisible hat. It is rather like the clouds that bring no rain.
You may have heard it said, Mr. Speaker, that farmers and others are sometimes caught between a rock and a hard place. I would submit that at the present time the farmers are not merely caught between a rock and a hard place, but are caught between an anvil and a hammer. The situation which many of them are facing is very drastic. Within the northwest region of Manitoba there are some 5,000 farmers. Many of them have been surveyed and at the present time 65 are in such desperate straits that they can get neither a bank nor a trade loan. In other words, there is no bank willing to give them credit in order for them to buy the seed they need to go on to the land. There are no companies prepared to give them the necessary loans to get into the seeding operation. These are the types of concerns I would like to underline as I speak on this motion put forward by my colleague.
It is often said that a picture speaks louder than words. I would like to share the type of representations I have been receiving on these matters that the farmers are facing. I have a letter dated April 19, 1984. This is another illustration of a farmer caught between the anvil and the hammer. This is a farmer who is being beleaguered by Revenue Canada. I would like to show you the repercussions that this type of thing has. This farmer writes:
I am a farmer and a school bus driver. As bus driver wages I earn about $6,000 which is certainly not enough for a family of five to live on. My gross farm income the last years has averaged about $20,000 with a net of about $4,000. I spend much more time working on the farm than the bus job. Besides, my wife and our older daughter do much farm work. Now I am being taxed on my farm home as though I am not a farmer. I am being penalized because I am not earning more on the farm than off the farm. How unjust can our tax system become. My family is working hard to make ends meet. Now, if I could net more income on the farm, I would have more money, but I wouldn't be taxed on my farm home. Gross injustice. What are you doing about this?
This is an illustration of the anvil and the hammer that the farmers are being caught between at the present time. I am receiving these letters on a daily basis. I have one dated April 24 which says:
I'd like to express my appreciation for what you are doing for us here in northern Manitoba. Also I'd like to express my concerns about the plight of many farmers in our L.G.D. of Mountain.
That stands for the local government district, Mr. Speaker. This is an area of municipal jurisdiction which does not have all the status of a municipality. The letter continues:
I thought it might be of interest to you to see how much land is up for tax sale in the L.G.D. It seems to me Mr. Whelan should be able to see that all is not well with the farm if every year there is a considerable increase in land going up for tax sale.
May 3, 1984

I counted the number of properties listed for sale for arrears of taxes in one small L.G.D. There are 34 municipalities in our constituency. I counted 56 pieces of propety in a small local government district which are up for tax sale.
As was mentioned earlier in the House today, there are many farmers who are concerned about increased freight rates. The worst fears of the farmers are being realized. According to a report in the Manitoba Co-operator:
Government officials said the 10 per cent safety net on the export basket price of grain won't be triggered by the projected increase.
A Government official said the process simply means farmers have more money in their pockets this year, but will have to pay it back in freight rates next crop year.
Some of these fears are plaguing many of the farmers because they cannot afford this. This is particularly true in constituencies such as mine where the average income of people is around two-thirds of the national average. This can represent a substantial loss to the farmers.
Perhaps you have been wondering whether I have been referring to people who are constantly writing to MPs. I just want to give you an illustration that there are many people who because of the drastic situation on farms are writing to me for the very first time in their lives. As a matter of fact, some of these people who are writing and phoning me as their Member of Parliament are contacting a Member of Parliament for the very first time. Another letter I have received reads:
I have never written to you before-
He goes on to say:
I do not like what is happening in Ottawa lately concerning the Western farmer-
He goes on to explain the expenses on the farm and the difficulty farmers are facing in these tough times. He continues:
Perhaps you have heard all about this before, but I think we should have ail or some of the federal or provincial taxes of gas, diesel, etc., removed. FCC should have more money given to them at lower interest rates-
He also comments on the Western Grain Stabilization Program and the necessity of amending this Bill so there would be a pay-out. Just to give you an indication, Mr. Speaker, of the type of alienation farmers are facing in western Canada, this individual goes on to state:
The Liberal Government does not care or knows nothing about what the West wants ... the Liberals have been in power for about 13 or 14 years and promised a lot of things for the west and we have seen very little done, mostly for Ontario and Quebec.
The lack of recognition for the needs of western farmers is something that I do not think has sunk sufficiently into the minds of Cabinet members.
I want to give you another illustration, Mr. Speaker, of the type of representation we receive. I am doing this basically to try to convince the Government of the types of problems the farmers have. I am going to read a resolution that was passed at a pot luck supper meeting held in Swan River. I pulled this
Supply
particular illustration from my riding because the Hon. Minister for Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has been to Swan River. In fact, this is where he got his green hat. I thought the Minister might be interested in knowing what the farmers who gave him the green hat have to say about his lack of involvement in dealing with agricultural problems. This is why I have chosen this illustration from Swan River from among the other representations I have received.
This particular resolution was passed on April 26. It was passed at a pot luck supper to which I was invited. It was an excellent meeting. Just for your edification, Mr. Speaker, I will indicate the way some of these rural people operate. Farmers and others brought food for the supper. As part of their own fund raising, they also collected a minimal sum at the door regardless of whether they brought food or not. It is almost a tradition. They invited me to speak. Once you speak you are subjected to questions and answers. These questions and answers go on for one or two hours. I think the Minister of Agriculture would be delighted to face some of these meetings. He would be able to understand some of the feelings and learn about the personal experiences of the farmers. These are not just statistics, they are personal experiences. This group made up of well over 100 people unanimously passed the resolution I will now share with you:
Whereas the Government of Canada has announced a payment of $300,000,000.00 from the Grain Stabilization Fund and Whereas this payment represents only the money farmers have contributed to the plan, and
Whereas this payment is intended to be made in October, and Whereas many farmers are in desperate need of Financing for current expenses of planting a new crop, and
Whereas farmers were promised from the outset of the plan that the Government would contribute $2.00 for every $1.00 farmers contributed,
Therefore be it resolved that the payout be increased to include an equal amount of Government money and be it further resolved that this payout be made immediately so as to assist farmers with their spring seeding expenses.
During the course of his speech the Minister of Agriculture, in response to some illustrations and examples which my colleagues from Saskatchewan gave, asked: what the provinces are doing. He seemed to indicate that the federal Government is doing everything for the farmers while the provinces are doing nothing. I want to correct that for the record. I want to give a couple of illustrations of what has been happening in Manitoba.
The New Democratic Government headed by Howard Pawley has been working diligently on the whole agricultural question. For example, the government has established a beef stabilization program. When this was introduced it was pooh-poohed. People said he would get no participation, that "Maybe you will get 7 per cent of producers participating", he said. But what has happened? Seventy to 75 per cent of the producers representing 70 per cent to 75 per cent of the province's livestock are in this beef stabilization program. Some $25 million has been given to this program.
Also a hog stabilization program at the provincial level has been introduced. Some $7 million has been expended on the program. The Manitoba Agricultural Credit Corporation has also been working very aggressively. It has been providing

May 3, 1984
Supply
loans to beginning farmers at reduced interest rates. We find in the interest relief reduction program that some 1,300 people have participated. Some $6.7 million has been expended at the provincial level. In addition, some farmers have been able to buy down their interest rates. This has helped farmers who have had ready cash and were caught in a high interest rate situation. They have been able to buy down the high interest rate. Some 600 people have benefited from that program.
If you were to take into account the amount of money which the provincial government has given by way of program or subsidy to the farmers in the two years the New Democratic Party Government has been in office, some 30,000 farmers have profited. The impact per average family farm has been $6,400. I would challenge the federal Government to match that type of assistance to farmers.
I see my time is coming to an end, Mr. Speaker, but I want to mention a few other points concerning the farm fuels sales tax and the well-head tax on farm fuel. At the same meeting in Swan River on April 26, another resolution was passed. Let me read it for the record:
Whereas some of the corporate fuel companies have reduced the cost of farm
fuels by 4.5 cents a litre or 20 cents a gallon if paid for within 30 days,
And whereas federal tax on farm fuels is high,
Therefore be it resolved that the federal government match the corporate oil
companies by eliminating the federal fuel tax.
Some companies have been taking this kind of action. The particular group assembled there have given this challenge to the Minister to respond in a favourable way. As I talk to many of the farmers in my riding, they tell me that their farm fuel bill has doubled in the last couple of years. There has been a tremendous increase in expense in farm fuels. For most farmers right now it is their number one cost. Many farmers had been involved earlier in loans and refinancing. For them, their number one cost is still interest rates. I want to emphasize the importance of this. As was mentioned earlier, we are always getting conflicting statistics from the Government as to what the exact amount is of the farm fuels sales tax. This is something which should be investigated and acted upon.
In conclusion, I should like to refer to a letter that I received from a farmer in the Swan River area. I use this as an illustration simply for the benefit of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). He wrote:
We are always told that our products have to compete on the world marketplace. But Sir, how can we compete when our own Government in its bid for taxes and power puts us farmers at a disadvantage? Just look at the price of fuel in the U.S.A ... Hope you don't think I'm a born complainer but unless the Government in Ottawa does some serious thinking about their policy, we will all go down like the Roman Empire.

speechtext: Questions or comments? The Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a comment rather than to put a question to the Hon. Member for Dauphin-Swan River (Mr. Lewycky), and he may want to add to it. I followed his remarks during the course of his speech and each time he referred to an increase in costs, I made note of it.
This is what I wrote down: a 15 per cent increase in Farm Credit Corporation interest rates. I do not know what has happened to the six and five as far as that corporation is concerned. Also he referred to a 30 per cent increase in grain freight rates. Again I do not know what happened to the six and five. Then he referred to a 35 per cent increase in fuel costs in the last few years; no six and five there either. I do not have the figure for fertilizer, but I understand that it has increased as well. There has been a continual increase in input costs. What effect is that having on farmers in the Dauphin-Swan River area?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that it is having a disastrous effect upon farmers in Dauphin-Swan River. As I indicated, based upon a survey conducted in my region, 65 farm families are in such dire straits that they cannot obtain money from any bank or trade company to put seed into the ground this spring.
Of course, farmers are very enterprising. I know members of their families will help them and chip in, but I am afraid that there will be an increased number of foreclosures and bankruptcies in my area. Our farms are not particularly large. They are not the size of those south of the Trans-Canada Highway. Farmers there are experiencing a very difficult situation. Unless there is some immediate pay-out from the Western Grain Stabilization Fund or some other action, I really fear for the farmers in my area. Once we take farmers off the land, city boys or girls will not farm land in rural areas. Any impressionistic or other observations I have made indicate that if we are to have a vibrant agricultural economy in our area, our farming sector, our vital food sector, will have to receive some kind of support. Farmers cannot really cope with these types of increases in our area.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Dauphin-Swan River (Mr. Lewycky) a question. A recent press announcement indicated that the Farm Credit Corporation was making available some $825 million this year in long-term loans and so on. If the Hon. Member were really doing his job by getting out and encouraging farmers in his area to take advantage of this long-term credit, he would know that this is the difficulty. At least in my area that has always been the problem. Of course, interest rates are a concern as well, but it is really important for farmers to obtain long-term credit. The FCC has that $825 million. I think it is a couple of hundred million more than it was a few years ago. I wonder whether the Hon. Member is really doing his job of ensuring that his constituency receives its share of long-term Farm Credit Corporation loans.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
My response to the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary is, yes, I have been doing my homework. I have talked with farmers about the Farm Credit Corporation. I have asked them to see the FCC people. They have told me that they are unable to obtain these loans and that they are far in excess of what they are able to pay by way of interest rates. They have told me that when the interest rate is compounded, they end up paying more than the 15 per cent.
May 3, 1984

Perhaps it is the Parliamentary Secretary who ought to be doing his own homework. He would see then that some action has been taken in this regard. Perhaps he should do that rather than shoot off his mouth glibly without having conducted any investigation on this issue. It is a major problem. We would not be receiving that kind of representation from people when we are talking to them in the coffee shops or wherever if it were not important. We have been talking to farmers in our area about that. Obviously he has not been doing his homework, if that is the kind of feedback he thinks he is getting.

speechtext: Are there further questions or comments? For debate, the Hon. Member for Welland.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one might ask why a Member of Parliament from southern Ontario who has largely a blue collar constituency would enter into this debate. I have farmers in my area, in the Niagara Peninsula, and as Hon. Members know, farmers are among the most productive sector throughout Canada.
The Hon. Member for Dauphin-Swan River (Mr. Lewycky) quite realistically put forward some of the problems in his area. I sympathize with the plight of some farmers in that area of Manitoba. There should be no doubt in the minds of anyone here that many farmers are under tremendous financial pressure. The extent of their difficulties varies depending on the individual, the size and type of the farming operation, the commodities produced and so forth.
Spring is traditionally a time for hope and new starts in the agricultural sector. Judging from the planting intentions of prairie farmers-and this is what the Hon. Member was talking about-there is hope for a good crop year. Recent surveys indicate that prairie crop producers expect to increase seeded acreage by 2.7 per cent over 1983 plantings. In March, a survey by Statistics Canada also indicated that Canadian farmers expect to increase fertilizer used this year by 4 per cent over 1983. Surely these are reasons for hope.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext: And the price has increased by 5 per cent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
Surely the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) will have his turn in a few moments. If he will let me share some of my information with him, perhaps he will be able to question me on it at the end of my remarks. I would be happy to answer his questions.
Hope alone will not help farmers to put in the new crop or keep them going until their livestock is ready for market. As we approach planting season, there is heightened concern about such mundane matters as cash flow and credit and, ultimately, who will make it through the season and who will not. We are dealing with a highly industrialized sector of the economy. I am talking about the farming industry, because many of the implements used by farmers are state of the art. Whereas it used to take thousands of men and women to man our farms, only between 4 per cent and 5 per cent of our entire population is involved in that industry at the present time.

The federal Government is aware of and extremely concerned about the Financial pressures and important decisions facing farmers at this time of the year. This is why we have taken a number of major initiatives over the past few months to help strengthen and support the financial position of Canadian farmers.
I would like to discuss some of these initiatives and explain some of the positive effects they have had and will have on Canada's agricultural economy, starting with some of the concrete financial assistance programs that have actually put cash in farmers' hands in recent months. One of the oldest and most reliable is the Agricultural Stabilization Program. Under the Agricultural Stabilization Act, we have been spending an average of about $350 million a year on stabilization payments for named and designated commodities.
Early in the winter, the $66.8 million stabilization program for eight designated commodities was announced. These commodities included 1982-83 crops of winter wheat, apples-I see the Hon. Member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King) is here; he would have an interest in that and can corroborate what I am saying-greenhouse cucumbers, onions, carrots, cabbages, rutabagas and white beans.
As of a week ago, the federal Government had processed claims and issued cheques to nearly 17,100 producers of those commodities. The accusations of the Hon. Member for Dauphin-Swan River are not totally accurate when he says we are not doing anything to help the farmers. I would also point out that all farmers do not live in the west. As I will point out in my speech, many farmers in Ontario, Quebec and, yes, even the Maritimes, are going to be affected by the acts and actions of this Government.
In February, a support payment of $4.48 per tonne for the 1982-83 grain corn crop under the same Act was announced. Claims from some 1,200 corn producers have been processed to date. In total, the federal Government expects to pay out $14.8 million to corn producers this spring. About 80 per cent of that will go to Ontario farmers. We have a broader spectrum here than just the farmers of the west. Our farmers are situated in every province of this country.
Other federal programs have put money into the pockets of the fruit growers this winter. This is where I become involved. In our area, the Niagara Peninsula, where we grow such fruits as apples, pears, peaches and, of course, grapes-we produce 80 per cent of the grapes of Canada and 80 per cent of the wine in Canada-we are affected by what happens to the fruit growers.
In late December, cheques were delivered to all apple producers eligible under the Eastern Canada Apple Industry Compensation and Re-establishment Plan. Under this program growers whose orchards suffered frost damage could receive $40 per standard tree affected. This money will help them to re-establish their orchards this year. Meanwhile, British Columbia fruit growers received cash assistance under two other federal programs. One of these was a $4.84 million
3386

May 3, 1984
Supply
purchase and resale program to help the East Chilliwack Agricultural Co-operative process its 1983 raspberry crop. Under the other, the Agricultural Products Board agreed to buy up to $3.2 million worth of B.C. peaches and pears to help fruit growers in that province market their 1983 crop.
These are positive things that the Government has been doing. We should be telling Canadian farmers and the public at large about these. All of those programs have helped to improve the cash flow situation of the participating farmers, providing them with funds with which to pay their bills and purchase inputs for the 1984 planting season. I hope we will hear more about this as the debate continues in the House today.
On April 1 the federal Government increased the target returns level for industrial milk and cream production by 1.5 per cent, from $43.18 per hectolitre to $43.83 per hectolitre. This increase will help dairy farmers cover higher production costs. Changes to yet another program will help Newfoundland livestock feeders. I am referring to the increase in feed freight assistance rates to all destinations in Newfoundland. This was announced a mere two weeks ago.
Agriculture Canada spends over $1.2 billion annually to assist the nation's agri-food industry. Many of the programs funded by the Department are aimed directly at farmers. Among these is the federal-provincial crop insurance program. The federal Government contributes around $150 million a year to this important and successful program.
Under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, we make it possible for farmers to borrow more than $200 million a year, with the interest rates being at a lower rate than would otherwise be possible because the federal Government guarantees these loans. The federal Government also helps farmers' cash flow situation through to advance payments programs. In total, about $500 million a year is advanced to farmers, with the Government paying the interest charges. This allows them to pay their bills and market their products in an orderly manner.
A couple of months ago the Government introduced Bill C-23 to amend the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act. The Hon. Member for Dauphin-Swan River alluded to that in his remarks. Under the proposed amendments, the maximum advance for individuals will double from $15,000 to $30,000. Emergency advances will also increase. Both Opposition Parties have expressed support for this Bill. I am hopeful that it can be passed in the very near future.
While we are talking about programs in support of prairie crop producers, I want to mention initial grain payments. The initial payments for spring wheat, Durum and designated barley will decrease this year, that is true. However, initial payments for feed oats, feed barley and designated oats will increase from 1983 levels. These levels are, of course, based on world grain markets. However, you can be sure that it was the Government's intention in setting these prices to help farmers as much as possible to maintain cash flow.
This discussion of initial grain prices brings us to another important program for the prairie grain producer. I mention this because some Members on this side have been paired with western ridings so that they can have direct input to our caucus. I am paired with the riding of Wetaskiwin. The Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) stepped out of the Chamber for a minute. I am sure he will be back. This discussion of initial grain prices brings up the matter of the other important program for prairie grain producers. One program that has been debated this afternoon is the Western Grain Stabilization Act. In the Speech from the Throne in December, it was announced that the Government would be looking at ways to make the Western Grain Stabilization Act more responsive to the needs of producers. In January, we lowered the level of producer contributions to the program from 2 per cent to 1.5 per cent of eligible receipts. Just eight days ago the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of State responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board announced proposed amendments that would make the program more flexible and more responsive to the needs of the grain producers. At that time they also outlined the key changes Parliament will be asked to approve. This is a lot of quick action on a major program in a very short time, yet we hear calls for a large initial payment from the program immediately. It takes time. It has to filter through the system. I am sure we would all like to see a pay-out from the fund as soon as possible to help farmers with their seeding cost. However, the formula will not trigger a payment until the laws governing the programs are changed. That is what we hope to do in this Parliament as soon as we can.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Hovdebo:
That his House recognizes the tremendous financial difficulty that farmers have been placed under and therefore recommends that the government immediately consider injection of much needed cash into farming through:

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject we are debating today is certainly not new. The subject, in perspective, is simple, namely, interest rates. In listening to the discussions in this House today, my mind went back to the introduction of the Western Grain Stabilization Act some seven years ago. I remember at the time trying to understand the formula. I expressed my concerns at that time in the House to the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board. I said, "There is no one who can understand the formula. It will not work". He said, "I understand it and it will work". Seven years later, we are back to reality.
May 3, 1984

As one of my colleagues said a moment ago, the happiest guys in western Canada are the ones who stayed out of the plan. It is essentially a lottery.
What the Government has done in this academic-type of formula is to average out a farm area which extends a thousand miles east and west. There are whole sections in that farm area which have had two, three, four or five bad years in the last seven years, yet the farmers there are not allowed to collect. The plan is based on an average over the whole area- the largest, homogeneous agricultural area in the world.
That was the fault of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act of 1938. That Act was scrapped in 1957 and replaced with a crop insurance program. Any pretence in the House that legislation, which was brought forward to cope with the difficulties under the Western Grain Stabilization Act, will be resolved in the next two or three weeks and presented to the House is nothing but sheer, unadulterated fraud and scam. It would take the best brains in the world to improve this Act to make it work. That is why my colleague was quite wise when he said a moment ago that the luckiest guys are the ones who did not join the plan. They can take the amount of their contributions, put them out at bank interest, and have three times as much coming as the Government is attempting to provide under these amendments. It is the farmers' money. They do not even use government money.
In my area, we passed a resolution on this nine months ago. We knew the Government's plan would not work. We decided to pass out all of the money, have the interest come back, and we would do our own stabilization. We decided to let the nitwits in Ottawa spend the next 100 years trying to figure out a new formula that would work. It would take them that long when dealing with such a vast agricultural area where the weather cannot be controlled by public servants or by Ministers.
The motion by the NDP is very timely and supports what has been going on on this side of the House for four years. I went back and looked at a motion brought to the House three years ago by the Conservative Opposition, dated June 1, 1981. It read:
-extending the Small Business Development Bond to unincorporated farmers,
That was part of the Budget of the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), under the administration of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), which set up the small business development bond concept. The motion was rushed through and became law before the Government was defeated. It applied that principle to individuals as well as incorporated individuals and incorporated companies. It was a motion put forward on June 1, 1981, by the Official Opposition in answer to the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) request of the Opposition that it put forward ideas which would be helpful and constructive, ideas which the Government could act on. That was the first proposal.
The second proposal was to amend the Farm Credit Corporation Act, the Agricultural Stabilization Act and the capital gains tax to ensure that Canadian farmers had access to
Supply
necessary and sufficient funding. Those were the general resolutions put forward in a motion by the Opposition on an Opposition Day three years ago less one month. The next year, the Government brought forward amendments to these pieces of legislation. That was on March 30, 1982-two years plus a couple of months ago.
The Government brought in legislation. One piece dealt with the Farm Credit Corporation to get away from the high interest rates that the Treasury of Canada was charging the Farm Credit Corporation. The Bill recommended that the Farm Credit Corporation be allowed to borrow money by any means. I stood in the House and congratulated the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) that he should be so lucky as to have an amendment before him that allowed him to do anything he wanted in order to get interest rates down. He accepted that praise. He went on television and made a statement that he would be doing that immediately. That was in 1982. It was two years and two months ago that all this happened. The Minister stood in this House today and said that even if the Bill did come before the House and the amendments were passed, the Government would still be unable to make a payment until the fall, and then only a small fraction of it because the Government cannot bend the formula too much.
Seven years ago, when this Bill originally came out, I wrote to my constituents and recommended that they stay out of the plan. I told them that it was like a lottery and that the only people who should participate are young farmers, farmers so young that they might live until they are old enough to have a chance in a million of getting something out of it. I suggested that they should start farming at 15 and plan to die at 75. It is a matter of luck. They are gambling on the weather as well as everything else which affects the growing of crops.
I do not want to push the point too far, but this was lousy legislation from the very beginning, supported by academic minds going back to Cornell University 60 years ago. My God, the Minister had to stand and take the rim-rocking he took today. He spread through this Chamber vapours of fertilizer that covered the whole area for an hour, but it still is fertilizer.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that the farmer is meeting a cash flow situation, and not just in the west where the western grain stabilization is in effect, but all across the country. His gross income is steady, but the cost inputs have risen so dramatically during the last seven or eight years that even the most efficient farmer in the world cannot accomplish a net gain because there is a cost in there which grew over which he had no control. It was foisted on him by a government which pushed the banks into a deliberate policy of high interest rates thought up by the morons in the Bank of Canada and the Department of Finance who believe you can stop inflation by raising interest rates. Exactly the opposite is the truth, Mr. Speaker. I have said in this House over and over again that interest rates are the main cost. Interest rates are the inflation.

May 3, 1984
Supply
If one looks at the figures for 1982, one sees that every large corporation in Canada averaged out all its costs. If you isolate the main cost, you find that 62 per cent of all the costs of every major corporation in Canada in the year 1982 was in interest. If that does not get through the fog, the brick wall which surrounds the minds of these mandarins who follow a theory which was proven wrong 30 years ago, then this country is doomed, as is the United States and all of Europe as we follow willy-nilly this nonsense that the civil servants of all our countries can plan so much better than the individual. That is the issue here. I would say that this motion, put into this perspective, serves once again, Mr. Speaker, to remind the people who are listening, reading, watching and worrying, that there is still hope.
This Parliament has amended the Farm Credit Corporation Act which enables that corporation to borrow money at half the interest rates and lend it out at half the interest rates, not costing the federal Treasury a nickel but ensuring that there is fair value for the money. In the original Farm Credit Corporation Act we charged the farmers by statute a maximum of 5 per cent. This Government, which has been in office for the last 20 years, ignored that statute, ignored that pledge of honour to the farmers in all parts of Canada. Now there is a long-term interest rate of 15 per cent, Mr. Speaker.
We must honour this Minister, who is not an evil man. He would do the right thing if he only knew what it was. He was all for the Farm Credit Corporation Act three years ago when he introduced it. All Parties supported him in 1982 when it was suggested that it be amended. He said he was going to do it. Why has he not? Because there is another clause in that legislation which says, "With the approval of the Department of Finance". You can understand now, Mr. Speaker, the candidate for the Leader of the Liberal Party when he says, "When I become Prime Minister I want to be able to fire Ministers of Finance which ignore Parliament". Well, he can start right now. There are three of them all along the line, such as, for example, the Hon. Mr. Turner, the Hon. Jean Chretien, and I am naming them just to make it clear. They are now candidates. Four successive Ministers of Finance have bent their knees to the dictates of a few in the Department of Finance who say that they and God walk alone with the truth.
It is not a new phenomenon. It happens all over the world. When Ministers, and ex-Ministers particularly, get down to talk to their counterparts from all the countries of the world, whether it be Russia, China, the United States, Great Britain, France or Italy, it does not make any difference to the civil servants which Party is in power. They call the tune. That is the real issue we are facing across Canada and in many other nations. When are we going to tackle this mythology that only the elite can rule, the self-styled elite? They actually believe religiously that once you graduate from a well-known university, climb up the ladder with your nose in the right attitude and arrive at the right place, you alone speak with God.
On this particular motion, I know where the hearts of every Member of Parliament are. We are all together on this issue, whether we are Liberal, NDP or Conservative, but the time
has to come sooner or later when Cabinet Ministers are willing to resign their positions if Parliament's wishes are being changed. Until a Cabinet Minister is willing to resign on principle and say why, there will be no change.
That is the question which should be asked of these candidates who are running for the leadership of the Liberal Party today. Are they going to volunteer to resign if they become leader and Find themselves overruled by their own employees? That is the tragedy of what we are witnessing today. This is not a matter just for farmers. It is a matter for small-businessmen, young people trying to buy a home, older people as well as people trying to go into the export business with the great risk and uncertainty that goes with it. Even the great and the mighty are on their knees: Massey-Ferguson, International Harvester, General Motors, Ford. You never saw such great enterprises coming to Government so fast to get help. The fact is that we are not fighting a mist, we are fighting a belief, a single belief which is quantitatively wrong. Therefore, let us, as Members of Parliament, once again reassert the dominance which the people have given us by electing us and say that we are willing to vote against our own Party, that we are willing to resign from positions of power, if Parliament's wishes are broken. But Ministers just seem to accept this situation. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has apologized to this House. Parliament has said that all children, orphans or not, have equal right to family allowances. Yet regulations put through by Order in Council, which the Ministers do not know anything about, said that neither orphans nor pregnant teenage girls can get family allowance. Who else in Parliament has stood up with me and kept pounding at that issue? There are no votes among the orphans who are under 18. And here is a similar case where the will of Parliament, supported by all Parties of this House in 1982, on the question of interest rates, on these four subjects, is being flouted and ignored, and the Minister does not even know it.
There was an advertisement which appeared three weeks ago in all the rural papers of Saskatchewan with the picture of the Minister of Agriculture. He is preaching the views of the experts in his own Department. I do not know whether or not he read it. He is talking to the people of Saskatchewan, and this is what he said:
World demand for grains and oilseeds is expected to increase by up to 50 per cent in the next 10 years.
There are also new markets appearing for our meat products in many Pacific countries too.
It is exactly the opposite, Mr. Speaker, of what his colleague in the other place is telling the farmers and what the Minister said today. There is a great future for agriculture in every country of the world! The Minister knows it. We all know it. There is a great future for our forest and fibre industries, as well as our fish industry. Everyone knows it. The World Food Council has been warning the world, asking us to rally our strength and produce all we can. There will be money made by all countries out of this. Yet we cannot change the law. My God, all you need do is to bring in an item in the Estimates,
May 3, 1984

get it through and you will correct it when you get around to changing the law. They do it all the time.
To sit here as a representative of a rural area and have to listen to that claptrap, Mr. Speaker, comes real hard. I have looked into the faces of these farmers who have fought so hard to get up and going these last 30 years. They have seen all they fought for put in danger today because the Government would not follow the laws of this Parliament which allows them to cut interest rates in half and no one loses any money.
I speak with some feeling, Mr. Speaker, because I have dealt with this subject for many decades. But I say to this House once again that there is no place for any one of us to hide on this issue.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Bachand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take this opportunity to inform the House about what the Government has done for farmers over the past years through the Farm Credit Corporation. 1 realize there are still some serious problems in the agricultural industry, but the situation is not as gloomy as some people would have us think. The federal Government is providing substantial assistance to Canadian farmers who are suffering the effects of the present economic situation. The Government's intervention is not a temporary affair but goes back to 1929, when the Canadian Farm Loan Board was created to help farmers who were unable to obtain all the long term farm credit they needed. The Board and its successor, the Farm Credit Corporation, have been meeting farmers' needs for 55 years now.
To give Hon. Members an idea of the funds invested by the Corporation in farming, the Corporation now has about 79,300 active loans, representing a total investment of $4.7 billion at this time. This clearly represents a substantial contribution to the financial well-being of Canadian farmers. During the Financial year ending on March 31, 1984, the Corporation approved some 5,736 loans under its regular credit program and the special Farm Financial Assistance Program, totalling $758 million, which represents an increase of $141 million over the previous year. Not long ago, the Government approved a budget for approximately $825 million, the funding that will be available to the Farm Credit Corporation for loans to Canadian farmers in 1984-85.
The mission of the Farm Credit Corporation is to help young farmers and farmers who are just starting, in other words, farmers whose assets are not sufficient to serve as collateral for loans from commercial lenders. The Farm Credit Corporation plays a vital role. Young farmers and owners of small, developing farms are far more vulnerable than estab-
Supply
lished operations. They have fewer assets but need considerable capital to establish and maintain a viable operation. Furthermore, they must be able to borrow capital on favourable terms, something the commercial sector is unable to provide. In fact, the floating interest rates or rates adjustable at frequent intervals that are offered by the commercial sector do not take into consideration the particular constraints of the agricultural sector.
Throughout the Canadian labour force, the only people who are really suited to primary farm production and who are anxious to work in this area are the sons and daughters of farmers. They are, in fact, the only people with a knowledge and practical experience of farming.
We must therefore facilitate the transfer of farm operations to the younger generation, so as to keep this human resource in the farming sector, and maintain and increase productivity in the agricultural industry.
This will happen only if we offer interest rates at reasonable levels as well as favourable credit terms, something commercial financial institutions normally do not do.
In addition, family farms are transferred gradually. In general, the son or daughter will purchase the farm bit by bit while acquiring the assets and experience needed. Eventually, they take over the whole operation. As the land itself is the basic requirement for most farm producers, beginners generally need credit to purchase land. On the average, farm real estate represents close to 80 per cent of total investment needs in agriculture. Credit requirements for land purchases are therefore very high. While parents generally want to help their son or daughter get established on the farm, they must recover the assets accumulated in their farm to be able to retire, or to distribute their property equitably amongst the family members. Even young people who are getting started with the assistance of their family will therefore need credit on terms not generally offered by the business sector. This is where the Farm Credit Corporation comes in. At the present time, the FCC offers the farm community loans of up to $350,000 or $600,000, depending on whether the operation involves one or more eligible applicants.
The Farm Credit Corporation loan limits were increased twice during the last three years to meet the needs of farmers more adequately. In view of the special financing requirements of farm operations, the Government has offered them, by way of the Farm Credit Corporation, long term farm credit programs on terms not generally available either to them or to other small businesses, to promote farm production. These terms include mortgages at interest rates frozen for Five, ten or thirty years, repayment periods of up to thirty years, flexible repayment schedules, a recovery policy which takes into account temporary financial problems and the cyclical nature of farm income, loans of up to 100 per cent of the assets stated as equity as well as a financial advice and consultation service for farmers.

May 3, 1984
Supply
The Farm Credit Corporation puts a lot of energy into its consultation services program because the farmer needs a sound understanding of financial management in order to succeed. The FCC offers advisory services at the preliminary stage, when the loan is approved and at various subsequent stages. While financial advice is available to all farmers, the FCC concentrates on its new borrowers or on other borrowers in need and those who request assistance.
The purpose of the advisory services offered by the FCC is to help farmers manage the financing of their operations in such a way as to eventually reach their personal and economic goals.
The FCC borrowers who need advice are generally those with limited assets and a high level of indebtedness, with an expanding operation but little experience, with a high-risk operation or financial difficulties. The credit advisors of the FCC provide borrowers with the assistance they need to start a bookkeeping system, and to interpret and analyze financial data so that they can identify and solve problems as soon as these crop up. Borrowers normally follow the program for two or three years. This is long enough for them to learn to manage their financial affairs efficiently. As of March 31, 1984, 4,800 borrowers were registered in the consultation services program, which accounts for 30 per cent of all FCC borrowers.
In addition to managing these credit programs, the FCC co-operates with other federal agencies and departments, provincial governments and private credit institutions to meet the special needs of the agricultural industry. For several years now, it has been co-operating with the Provinces of Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Alberta and has been involved in their interest subsidization programs. The FCC has intensified its efforts in this field in 1982 and 1983 by being involved in the Saskatchewan farm purchasing program as a lending institution.
Last year, the FCC signed an agreement with the Province of Ontario to act as a lending institution under the assistance program for new farmers.
The FCC lends to farmers who represent high risks for the private sector. A survey carried out by the corporation has shown that the average Canadian farm had net assets of 85 per cent. On the other hand, those farmers who obtained a regular loan from the FCC had net assets of nearly 50 per cent in the last five years. The average net assets of farmers who obtained a loan under the special Farm Financial Assistance Program were even lower, namely 35 per cent in the 1983-84 fiscal year and 40 per cent in the previous year.
The loan-to-equity ratio is also indicative of the risks involved. As the FCC was authorized in 1975-76 to lend up to 100 per cent of the value of the property offered as equity, the loan-to-equity ratio is increasing. The FCC has granted a
greater percentage of its loans to farmers who offer less equity than in the past. This tendency to lend to farmers with lower net assets and a higher loan-to-equity ratio results from the fact that the corporation is lending to younger farmers with limited resources, and also from the difficult economic situation.
The special Farm Financial Assistance Program was reintroduced in the June 1982 budget. Loans to farmers under 35 continue to account for the larger part of the funds loaned by the FCC, making up 62 per cent of the total. Most of these farmers own little land and have few personal assets. Whether they want to get into farming or to extend their operation, these young farmers must borrow larger amounts for longer periods. Many of them, especially those who must consolidate their debts, cannot offer additional equity, which means an even higher loan-to-equity ratio.
As Hon. Members are aware, the FCC has administered the special Farm Financial Assistance Program since its implementation in November 1981.
Under this program, farmers facing financial disaster were offered for a two-year period an interest rebate on their loans from the FCC. Parliament allocated funds to the FCC to cover the rebate guaranteed on these special loans.
When the program was launched in November 1981, the Government had set aside an overall budget of $50 million, including $5 million for interest rebates of 5 per cent, the key element. The funds earmarked for the program were soon exhausted and it ended on March 31, 1982.
This time the interest rebate has been set at 4 per cent and the $200 million allocated to the program have made it possible to pay out $16 million in interest rebates. The program was renewed in the April 1983 Budget with an additional $100 million Government commitment.
Between November 1981 and March 31, 1984, the Farm Credit Corporation spent in excess of $341 million under this program and more than 2,200 Canadian farmers had received or are still receiving assistance thanks to the program.
When the program was set up, the Government was expecting the economy to pick up steam during the two-year rebate program. We all know that the recovery was sluggish in the agricultural sector, and the Government is now considering the possibility of extending the rebate period or other mechanisms to help farmers who are still strapped for cash. As the Minister pointed out, a decision will be made soon.
Mr. Speaker, I should emphasize that the role of the Farm Credit Corporation is to make mortgage loans available only to those farmers who are now considered as high risk ventures. The Farm Credit Corporation was not established to assume the responsibilities of the banks or extend credit to commercial agricultural operations. In the late seventies, when the agricultural economy was booming, commercial lenders asked for a larger slice of that market. Despite a decline in agricultural
May 3, 1984

activities, I expect that they will continue to make farm loans. The Government is keeping a close watch on long-term agricultural loan market trends and is considering various alternatives to provide funding for the Farm Credit Corporation. For its part, the FCC is now seeking ways to reduce rates on those high interest loans. The Government is firmly committed to support the agricultural community and we are trying to find the best means to shore up that industry just as it is getting out of the doldrums.
I should like to remind Hon. Members that the Farm Credit Corporation is one of the very few lending institutions whose loan recovery policy is geared to the cyclical nature of farm income. As long as an agricultural operator stands a reasonable chance of pulling himself out of a precarious financial situation, the FCC will give him free rein.
The federal Government helps Canada's agricultural community through credit programs on which farmers can rely to make their operations more profitable. It is through the Farm Credit Corporation long-term mortgage loan programs and the medium-term loan program under the Farm Improvement Loans Act that the federal Government makes sure that Canadian agriculture remains one of the most efficient and most productive sectors of our economy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to be able to participate in this debate inasmuch as it affects the area which I represent, namely, that of Okanagan-Similkameen. I congratulate you on your correct pronunciation, Mr. Speaker. Some others have failed in that regard.
The farmers in Okanagan-Similkameen, and in British Columbia as a whole, face, I believe, the most desperate circumstances of any farmers in all of Canada. Therefore, it is appropriate that we speak to this resolution today.
I have in my possession a letter which I recently received from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), which begins with this statement:
It was with some dismay that I read a report in the British Columbia Grower's News, entitled "M.P. Raps Government" ... the report cites statements by you criticizing the scarcity of funds available through the FCC and the outrageously high rate of interest for what loans the corporation does make.
The letter goes on to say:
1 would like to take this opportunity to inform you of some of the things Agriculture Canada and the Canadian Government have done, and are doing, for the fruit farmers of British Columbia.
I believe he must have circulated his three-page letter to everyone in his caucus because there has been a repeated recitation of the points made in the Minister's letter to myself. The Minister is certainly justified in explaining to me, to the House, to Canadians, and to the world-wide constituency, of which he is so pleased to speak and which he claims to
Supply
represent at every opportunity, the contributions of the federal Government to Canadian agriculture. No one disputes that. Likewise the farmers of Canada, and of British Columbia in particular, are justified in telling the Minister of the areas in which he is failing them. They are significant to their difficulties.
In the statement recently circulated by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, which deals largely with farm credit, a number of resolutions and points are made to which the Minister, I think, should pay attention because they would assist the farm community. The Federation of Agriculture had a resolution about the elimination of the 9 per cent federal sales tax on farm fuels. We agree with that. It speaks of Section 31-restricted farm losses and the application of that section. We agree with that. It speaks of amendments to the capital gains tax law. It speaks of duties and sales taxes on imported agriculture products. It speaks of tariff protection. It speaks of stabilization payments. Most specifically, it focuses on the Farm Credit Corporation, its policy and the ability of the FCC to address the concerns of the Canadian farmer.
Yesterday, Mr. Jack Wessell, General Manager of the British Columbia Federation of Agriculture, together with Mr. Harold Allison who comes from my riding, a rancher of note, Vice-president of the B.C. Federation of Agriculture and Chairman of the B.C. Cattlemen's Committee, were in Ottawa bringing a message of special concern from B.C. farmers of the very special and damaging circumstance with which B.C. farmers must contend, circumstance which this Government and this Minister seem inclined to ignore and gloss over in their statements and policies. These deal with the high cost of labour, land, equipment and supplies, which are the highest costs in Canada. In many cases they are the highest costs in the world.
I would like to point out to the House and to the Minister, because I know he will read my speech with rapt attention, the labour situation that exists in British Columbia. This is an area with a highly organized labour force. Farmers in British Columbia must compete with other areas of employment. Just last week we met with a group of mining executives from British Columbia who pointed out to us that the costs of mining in British Columbia are the highest in the world. The labour costs in British Columbia mining are the highest in the world. In the forest industry in British Columbia the situation is the same. The labour costs are the highest in the world. In transportation as well the labour costs are the highest in Canada and perhaps in the world. And then we have food merchandising. Let me read from the March 1984 issue of Country Life, which is British Columbia's agricultural newspaper. The article reads:
According to a recent article in the Vancouver Sun, these food workers are now approaching the second year of a two-year agreement which saw wages rise 85 cents an hour last year, and will see wages again rise 76 cents to 83 cents this April.
These raises will bring the hourly wages of a part-time clerk stocking shelves in the store to $16.78 an hour, while full-time clerks in the same category will earn $618 for a 40 hour week: a total of $32,136 a year.

May 3, 1984
Supply
It goes on to explain that on top of that there is an additional about 40 per cent in benefits. The article continues:
To add insult to injury, a comparison of the wages of the retail employees to similar employees in other parts of North America is in order.
It goes on to compare the $16 an hour in B.C. for food handlers to the $12 in Ontario. It is much less in Manitoba and much, much less in the State of Washington, U.S.A. The writer of this article states:
! don't think it is hard to understand why local fruit growers only receive less than five cents a pound for apples, while consumers pay more than 50 cents a pound.
That is the cry of agriculture in general. Why can we not get more of the money which the consumer pays? The Minister knows that these circumstances exist and that they plague B.C. agriculture. He has been there. He has met with farmers in British Columbia.
A few weeks ago I participated in a meeting in Kelowna at which the Minister met representatives of the B.C. fruit tree industry. This meeting was a direct result of representations which I made to the Minister following a very dramatic Labour Day rally in Penticton at which nearly 1,000 farmers, many with tractors and trucks which tied up highway traffic, took their protest to the public.
During the meeting with the Minister, one intelligent, industrious, keen orchardist-and I see the Minister coming into the House and he will remember that man-explained the situation of high costs. I think it was Rob Dawson who indicated to the Minister the high level of wages which must be paid to Okanagan farm labour, high in comparison with other areas of Canada and in comparison with other competing areas in the world. He posed a question to the Minister: How do we survive in this circumstance? I remember well the Minister's response. He said, "I hope you are not suggesting that you should pay lower wages". I am sure the Minister remembers that. Of course, that is not the position which the farmers of B.C. take. We know that farm workers are not overpaid for what they do. We know that we must maintain wage scales competitive with other segments of the B.C. economy if we are to have labour on farms.
I recite this episode because it demonstrates an absolute contradiction in the position which the Minister is taking with respect to the B.C. farm community. On the one hand he says, as he did to Rob Dawson in Kelowna, "I hope you are not suggesting that you should pay lower wages", in other words go on paying the highest farm wages in the world. Go on paying for all the social benefits which are demanded as part of your employment payments. Go on paying the highest cost for agricultural land in Canada. Go on paying the highest costs for water, power, services, farm equipment and supplies. In telling the farmer to keep on paying these highest costs, the Minister contradicts his position as indicated in his statement on stabilization. Now he changes his tune and says that he recognizes no differences in input costs and that stabilization is at the same level from coast to coast. Not only did he state that, but he indicated that if a provincial Government recognizes that these cost differences exist and does something to
assist farmers to cope with higher costs, the federal Government will penalize them. In other words, he is saying that if the Province of British Columbia helps farmers to stay in business, to keep from going bankrupt, to pay their bills and labour costs, the federal Government will penalize them by refusing them stabilization. Mr. Wessel and Mr. Allison came to Ottawa to plead with the Government on behalf of B.C. farmers. They wanted the Government to recognize the circumstances because if it did not B.C. farmers could not exist. I suppose we could say, so much for co-operative federalism, so much for the philosophy or the attitude of the man who has hopes to lead the Liberal Party!
Only a few days ago we heard an Hon. Member on the government side talking in the House about getting payments out when they should get out. We should get them out to the people when they need them. At that time I rose to speak about the Minister's kind letter to me in which he mentioned stabilization payments being made on behalf of apple growers for the 1982 crop. It was marvellous, but the problem was that the payment came in 1984. We must remember that farmers started having input costs to produce their 1982 crop in November, 1981. Many farmers have told me, the Minister and anyone who would listen, that by the time the payment arrived they had used up most of its benefit in bank interest. They should get the payment out when it is helpful. I am sure the Minister appreciates that. Farmers appreciate it when it comes in the form of a cheque with a date that means something to them.
The Minister is aware of some of the irritants affecting farmers. We should not be nit-picking over detail when they are in trouble. I am thinking of the protest in the Okanagan which was brought to the attention of the Minister at a meeting in Kelowna. I know it is a tough, controversial issue. It concerns retroactive changes to the crop insurance program which prejudice the interests of orchardists who signed up in good faith and discovered later that the program had changed. I believe it was pointed out to the Minister that some $1 million was involved or had been reduced from payments made to farmers who were already in deep trouble. Many of them will probably be unable to survive.
I had occasion to meet with guests today from the Okanagan who told me that three or four orchards in south Okanagan have gone into receivership or bankruptcy. They told me about their peach operations, how advance payments were made and then at the end of the season they had to repay money to the packing house which advanced payments, through the federal Government program I admit. The payment from the market to peach growers in the Okanagan was $58.84 per tonne. This is what the selling agency was able to send to packing house organizations for distribution to growers. However, it cost about $400 per tonne to produce the crop. Certainly their costs are higher than in other areas of Canada, but these are the facts.
May 3, 1984

How can the Minister justify saying to farmers faced with deficits that he knows it costs $400 per tonne to produce peaches, that the market returns $58.84 per tonne, but if the provincial Government gives them any assistance, they will be penalized in the national interest? That does not make sense. No farmer in British Columbia will accept that philosophy, nor should they be asked to accept it.
Farmers know what appeared in the headlines of the Osoyoos Times over a dramatic picture of a dump truck dumping tonnes and tonnes of packed peaches last year because there was no market for them. Why was there no market? It was because the federal Government allowed imported peaches into the country as fresh fruit and in canned or processed condition. There were no hindrances. The anger of the farmers was demonstrated in the Labour Day rally. They asked for some protection to be provided, not against reasonably-priced products but against products that were dumped from other producing countries, notably Australia. The Minister knows the effect of Australian packed fruit, processed and canned fruit, in the Okanagan. It has resulted in the closing down of every cannery in the Okanagan Valley but one, and it is now in the process of being sold.

He talked about imports. He knows what representatives of his own province said when there was a discussion about controlling imports. They said that they could not do that because they exported lumber. He knows very well that they export apples to some 30 or perhaps 40 countries and have done so for years. When we talk about imports and exports, it is a two-way street. If we are to be rough on some imports, we can be sure that someone will be rough on our exports.
Also he talked about the crop insurance changes. He knows full well that the province initiated the changes in crop insurance. It was not the federal Government. We practically okayed what they wanted. The members of the advisory committee on crop insurance were asked what they thought about it, according to the records that I have, and they did not see much wrong with it, until they discovered that the new plan in some instances was not as good as the old one, and they wanted to change it back. When talking about controlling imports, I remember a provincial Minister in British Columbia saying that British Columbia was one of the biggest exporters of lumber and of other horticultural crops to other parts of the world.

I am sure the Hon. Member knows quite a bit about crop insurance. He was an agent for that federally-funded program. Imagine, that terrible federal Government! He was actually an agent selling that insurance where the federal Government funds 50 per cent of the premium, the producer pays the other 50 per cent, and the province administers the program. As an agent, he was paid for doing that.
The Hon. Member knows that stabilization is not the same from coast to coast, unless it is a nationally-marketed commodity. There are eastern and western regions for stabilization. The Hon. Member could have read the whole letter and stated how many millions of dollars I was able to send to the two different groups. I am going by memory, but I believe it was a total of $8 million to buy surplus products in their warehouses so there would not be distressed selling. That money was provided interest-free. When you add all that we spend in British Columbia, you find that we care as much about agriculture in that province as does the provincial Government, and maybe a little bit more.
The Hon. Member talked about using income from the provincial plan. Does he not consider income from a government the same as income from a factory? He talked about treating people with equity. You have to take into consideration all of these programs. We offered 100 per cent income insurance under the stabilization program. That plan, which we offered federally, was superior to everything that British Columbia had, except the cow-calf program. They refused to join. They agreed that it was better for the other crops in British Columbia.
I repeat what I said earlier. We offered the plan, and not one province came forward and said it wanted the plan, that it would work out some kind of agreement. They did not accept it in 1977, but now they are asking for it. That is about all I want to say. I did not hear the rest of the Hon. Member's comments. You will notice that most of my comments were corrections to what he said.

Mr. Speaker, I wish the Minister had been here from the beginning because I did mention his letter. I said he was certainly justified in explaining to everyone the federal Government's contribution to Canadian agriculture, and nobody disputes that. I also said that farmers have an equal right and justification to tell the Minister the areas in which he is failing.
With respect to tariffs, let me read what the British Columbia Minister of Agriculture said. I quote the following from the Penticton Herald of September 9:
Agriculture Minister Harvey Schroder said Wednesday he is seeking imposition of temporary tariffs on imported fruits and vegetables when they are surplus in British Columbia. The request was made on an informal base to Federal Minister Eugene Whelan.
It is true that crop insurance changes did originate with the provincial Government. The provincial Government asked the Minister and the federal Government not to impose those changes for one year. The provincial Government, which ini-

tiated the changes after seeing the implications, asked that they be withheld for one year.
I do not remember the point that was made regarding stabilization. I do remember the Minister saying that everything the federal Government was offering was superior to anything available in British Columbia. In that circumstance, why then are the British Columbia Federation of Agriculture and the B.C. Cattlemen's Association here and why has the BCFGA made representations?
