speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to take part in this debate because of the importance of the agriculture sector and the resource sector. The summary of the challenges and choices which came from the royal commission headed by the Hon. Donald Macdonald was made available a week ago. It states that one of the challenges is the resources and the environment.
One challenge is to manage Canada's resources for maximum benefit over time and to ensure a pattern of development in harmony with enhanced environmental quality to continue the emphasis on the primary sector engine of economic growth. It stresses "to continue the emphasis". Under our very capable Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), this industry has gone forward. Unlike other sectors, we are subject to world economic conditions.
In his book entitled The Third Wave, Alvin Toffler points out that we can no longer isolate ourselves from the impact of conditions or policies that are put in place by other countries in the world. I look at this statement in the context of the huge surpluses and subsidies that are paid out in the European Common Market. I look at it in the context of the dropping commodity prices in the Canadian market. This is where we must look for assistance for Canadian farmers.
We have one of the highest standards of living of any country in the world. Consequently, we have set the precedent of a domestic price and an export price for some products that have been grown in Canada over the years. I believe that assistance to the farmers must come through the marketplace itself in co-ordination with the various policies that are brought forward by the Government and the Minister of Agriculture in particular.
I should point out that the sales tax which has been discussed here today is not a new tax that was brought in under the National Energy Program. That tax has existed for many years. In fact, the November, 1978 Budget reduced that tax from 12 per cent to the current 9 per cent.
To put this in perspective, I would like to place on the record some estimates of savings to farmers. After depreciation, fuel costs amount to a small percentage of a farmer's total costs. As a percentage of total costs after depreciation, fuel costs amount to approximately 8 per cent. Therefore, we are talking about a saving of a per cent of the cost of farm fuels, which account for 8 per cent of farm costs. In fact, we are talking about 9 per cent of 8 per cent. The excise tax on fuels is 1.5 cents per litre and is refundable upon application. This tax is not a net expense to the producer.
Another point I wish to make abundantly clear is that it is not only the federal Government that applies taxes to oil and gas producers. For example, in Saskatchewan, provincial royalties can be as high as 30 per cent although some wells and developments may enjoy three-year to five-year royalty holidays. Under the Oil and Gas Conservation Act in Alberta, a levy is imposed on the operators of oil and gas wells and oil
May 3, 1984

sands projects. This levy is basically a provincial Crown royalty on crude oil and gas, varying with production, based on a two-tier formula. This levy could amount to as much as 36 per cent, but at the present time is only 20 per cent.
On February 1, the Government of Canada reduced to zero the tax on natural gas and gas liquids. Was this saving passed on to the consumer? We must remember that farmers are consumers of natural gas as well. As most of us realize, natural gas is an ingredient of ammonia-based fertilizers. On checking the price of fertilizer, I have not found that it has decreased. In fact, the cost of natural gas to the consumer increased at the same time as this tax was removed.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, my question to the Opposition is, if this tax to which we are referring is reduced, will that benefit be passed on to the farmers? Can members of the Opposition give me the assurance that this will happen, or will the prices simply increase to make up the difference between what it is now and what it will be if the tax is removed? I know that they cannot assure me that this benefit will be passed on, yet they are basing their argument on the assumption that the price to the farmers will be reduced automatically if the tax is removed. It did not happen with natural gas and I would certainly want some assurance that it would happen in this case.
Opposition Members have not suggested that there should be a reduction in royalties and taxes at the provincial level as well. However, members of the Opposition did not mention what happened in Ontario when dye was introduced into farm fuel. The Ontario Minister of Revenue passed legislation two or three years ago which required that colour be added to the diesel fuel used in farm vehicles and tractors to distinguish between that diesel fuel and the diesel fuel used in highway vehicles. What happened when that was done, Mr. Speaker? A great many of my constituents suffered severe damage to their farm equipment. Not only were the filters on those tractors and combines plugged up, but in some cases the injectors and engines were ruined. The introduction of this dye was legislated a few years ago and that type of dye was only changed last year after tremendous expense to the producers. If that type of dye were to be used in the fuel for highway vehicles, I can imagine what would happen on our highways, especially during rush hour. However, there must be some way of distinguishing between the fuel used for food production purposes and the fuel used for highway vehicles.
One point that neither of the Opposition Parties mentioned is that as a result of the Government's pricing agreement on energy, there has already been a huge saving to the Government. This saving has affected not only Canadian farmers but all consumers, and it came about because of the blended energy price formula which was brought in under the National Energy Program. Opposition proposals would have created a higher price which, from what we understand, would have been effective until 1984. It is now the year 1984 and the Government's blended price is in place. That saving is accruing not only to the farming and producing sector but to our entire economy.
Supply
I believe that Canadian farmers should realize that there are other areas of savings that have been passed along to them. I would like to go one step further and point out to Canadian farmers that under the National Energy Program, we achieved self-sufficiency as of last November. Over 4,000 oil wells were drilled and completed in Canada in 1983. I am speaking now of oil wells and not of gas wells. Previously, the best year for the drilling and completion of oil wells was 1980, before the National Energy Program came into effect, at which time approximately 2,600 oil wells were drilled and completed.
I could go one step further and compare those figures with United States figures. The ratio is approximately the same. Approximately 10 times the number of wells were drilled in the United States during those same years as in Canada. The National Energy Program has been a success and has increased the level of Canadian ownership from approximately 28 per cent to 38 per cent.
The Government has moved in these areas to make sure that one of our strategic resources has been Canadianized. We have also made sure that we have become self-sufficient. Although we do not have a long-term security of supply in the oil sector yet, judging by the number of oil wells drilled and completed in Canada this year, we are well on our way toward achieving that security of supply.
We do admit that there has been a decrease in the number of gas wells drilled. In the Province of Alberta alone, there are something like 11,000 gas wells which are capped because the market for natural gas is not sufficient. Consequently, operators haved eased off on the drilling of gas wells. However, this has been a success, and I would like to indicate that there has been tremendous progress made since the federal Government introduced the National Energy Program.
I would like to reflect back just for a moment. I see here the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin). I know he would like to speak and I intend to give him ample time.
A little over two weeks ago I spoke in the House about the rural economy and the pressures that farmers are facing. I am well aware of the hardships, particularly those faced by farmers who do not have a large amount of equity in their operations-young people who are trying to get established. They are confronted with higher input costs on the one hand and lower receipts for the products they sell on the other. They are caught in a very difficult position. The Farm Credit Corporation, as was pointed out earlier today, has increased the amount of funding available to them. That is not the only answer. We must have in Canada a countervailing force in the marketplace to counteract the buying power of the very large retail chains which have formed buying groups to put pressure on the marketplace. In many cases it is fair to assume that producers' prices are set at the retail level and reflected downward-everyone else having a share of the profit if there is one. We have to re-examine the whole pricing sector in Canada if we are to achieve the maximum potential of our resource sector.

May 3, 1984
Supply
I said at that time that farmers should study the legislation available to them, both at the provincial and at the federal level to enable them to establish a price at the farmgate that would reflect their costs of production, plus a reasonable return on investment and labour.
I do not think there have been any suggestions presented here today or two weeks ago when there were two Opposition Days in the same week. I do not think any of the proposed actions, individually, will put the farm sector back on its feet. It has to be a co-ordinated effort involving programs put forward by the Minister of Agriculture. The House must consider some new programs, which I will speak about at another time. I have been in consultation with the Minister of Agriculture regarding some new proposals.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext: Are there any questions? Are we resuming debate? Resuming debate, the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments this afternoon on the motion, but I want to be fair to my hon. friend from the NDP who wishes to say a few words. I will attempt to split with him the time that is remaining. I know that the Minister, who is here, would like to hear both of us.
There is no end to the problems in the agricultural industry despite the fact that the Minister, in his condescending way, and the Member who has just finished speaking tell farmers how well off they are, how good they have it and how benevolent a government they have looking after their needs. This Government is managing the crisis in agriculture. It has and it will. There are no programs. There are no schemes. There is no light at the end of the tunnel. They are managing the crisis. And yet the farm economy in our country is measured by the bankruptcies that are experienced every year. It is measured by increases or decreases in the farm economy every year. The Minister and the $800 a day royal commissioner will tell us that we have to look at the history. At the turn of the century 49 per cent of the working population of this country was involved in some agricultural-related activity, today it is less than-what is it, Mr. Minister, 3 per cent?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext: It is 4.4 per cent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
It is 4.4 per cent. Well, it is less than 3 per cent in the United States. So I assume that the Government plans to reduce that percentage and reduce family farms-this rural, unsophisticated, smelly kind of business-to get on with concentrating and integrating farm operations. It will get into it in a big way because this Government obviously thinks that big is always better. The Government thinks that the family farm is really a way of life that belongs in the past. I say that it is not a way of life that belongs in the past, although I agree that it has become a very expensive way of life.
Farmers pay very dearly to live on the farm. They contribute much of their energy and resources to keep the family farm alive, despite the Government. Farmers throughout the country agree that it is high time and a matter of urgent
priority for Canadians to bring about a change in government. We need a government that is committed to a different set of priorities in terms of the industrial and economic structure of our country-priorities which put emphasis on the prime resource sectors of our economy; agriculture being the main pillar, along with mining, fishing and forestry. We must concentrate on our natural strengths once again and rebuild our economy that way. Only then can we pursue the high-tech, value added schemes for secondary manufacturing industries.
I would like someone to tell me, particularly the Minister of Agriculture who travels around the world, how are we to live with the high-tech revolution, our secondary manufacturing schemes, particularly in the aeronautics field? How are we to replace between $30 billion and $35 billion of foreign exchange earnings that are generated by agriculture, forestry and mining? It is a dream that is far in the future. We have to rebuild our prime resource sectors.
What are the problems in agriculture? It does not matter where you touch it, it is like an elephant. There is a problem everywhere you touch it. The key problems are laid out in this motion, the immediate pay-out of some of the Western Grain Stabilization Fund, which incidentally belongs to the farmers. There is no intention of paying out any of the Government's money, as I understand it, from this fund. All that is being paid out is the farmers' money.
When we are told there is a fund, I do not believe there is a fund. Certainly, there is a bookkeeping entry, but the money is in the Consolidated Revenue Fund of the Government. Of course, there is an accrual of interest, but there is not a fund. The Government has not paid into a fund. It is a bookkeeping entry. If the Government had paid into a fund it would have had to go elsewhere to borrow money to sustain its operations. Let us not be fooled about that. The Government has not been too generous. It does not pay anything toward this fund.
Why are we asking for an immediate pay-out of some of the Western Grain Stabilization Fund? The reason is that the average farmer in Canada does not have enough money to put in his crops. This, as it happens, is the season of the year when farmers put in their crops. I am sure that the Minister of Agriculture understands that. It is in the spring when crops are planted. Whether it is tomatoes or wheat, whatever is put in, it is usually put in at that time of year-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext: He is putting in a crop of a different kind.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
That is right. He is trying to seed a crop of a different kind. His harvest is on June 16. Indeed, it will be one of the earliest crops. It will be a hail-out.
We do not want to be unkind to you, Mr. Minister, but it is not funny. The farmers are in this kind of financial situation because of a number of factors. They have all been enumerated here today and will be again in future debates. The input costs have increased out of all proportion, and what is particularly serious about the input costs is that they are uncontrollable. I suppose that if you cannot afford a new combine, you
May 3, 1984

can always buy a used machine. There are all kinds of used farm equipment one can pick up at auction sales. In our part of the country, there are all kinds of auction sales and every morning when you turn on the radio you are told about at least five or six of them because farmers just cannot hack it any longer. So you have some control over that. You can delay purchasing a new combine and buy a used one. But there are certain costs, so-called input costs, over which you have no control, such as fuel tax, and related to that is the cost of fertilizer. For the Minister's edification, when you plant a crop you always put on fertilizer right after, so that is a cost which accrues to the farmer at this particular time, not in October when the Minister is planning to make a stabilization pay-out. They are faced with these costs right now.
I will tell the Minister something else. The suppliers who supply the fertilizer and the fuel, the bulk plant agent in the farm community, do not have the flexibility either to carry the farmer for these five or six months. There is no flexibility left in the small and medium-business sector. It needs its money now.
The former speaker said that farmers should not be so ungrateful but should look at what we have done. We have secured ourselves of enough energy for the future and, not only that, we have Canadianized the industry. We now own the industry. Well, a big help that has been to the farmers! We now own PetroCan. We have paid out $6 billion to own a part or a greater share of the Canadian energy sector. That $6 billion has had to come from somewhere, and the farmers are paying a big share of that $6 billion. Has it created a new barrel of oil? Has it created any jobs? Of course not. We have our priorities all wrong. We should have established some priorities to save the family farm. We should have taken $2 billion of that $6 billion to help the farm economy. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, the farmers have never asked to get anything for nothing.
We here in the capital decided that it is much better for us to have a so-called cheap food policy, that it is much better to make sure of our standard of living, and it is quite true, we do enjoy a very high standard of living in this country. However, I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, it is not owing to this Government. It is not owing to most of the other workers in our society. It is to the credit of our farmers who are working for nothing to grow cheap food so we have to spend only 24 per cent or 25 per cent of our disposable income on that commodity. That is not because of good management. That is because we have killed our farm economy and the farmers are working for nothing. They are not receiving any kind of return on their investment. Their investment is high. Land costs are very high. Machinery costs are very high. Yet the farmer still produces cheap food.
The Government says that if we did not have that cheap food policy and if the farmer were to get a return on his investment which is commensurate or equal to the return on the investment of any other industry, be it lumber or any other industry, food prices in this country would have to treble. That would happen if the farmer were to get a decent return on his investment similar to what is earned in any other industry.
Supply
Therefore, if the Government permitted that to happen, we would have to find some other way to help people buy food. We would need to have a sort of negative income tax or more welfare. Certainly, old age pensions would have to be doubled. That is the incredible situation which exists, and the Government has no flexibility, so it dumps it on the farmer. What makes it worse is that after having a cheap food policy in this country, we turn around and export that cheap food. We sell wheat and cereal grains below the cost of production everywhere in the world, to Japan, to Russia, and to the European Economic Community. A couple of years ago we sold barley to the European Economic Community. I believe it was at $ 140 a tonne. The European Economic Community knows that without a decent agricultural policy, if it relied on the rest of the world to provide it with its food, it would be in serious trouble. It is a sophisticated, modern industrial society, but it pays a lot of attention to its farm economy.
I do not know what the prices of barley are today. Perhaps the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) could tell us what they are a little later because he was involved with it on a daily basis, but two years ago the European Economic Community resold our barley. It bought it for $140 a tonne and resold it for $230 a tonne. Do you know what it did with the $90 profit? It gave it to its farmers in the form of a subsidy. That makes a lot of sense. We are the only innocent traders in the world. We are the only people, a lower middle power in terms of the industrial scheme in the world, who think that you should give away food. We think we should not enter into supply-management arrangements with foreign countries to protect our own interests. We think we should give everything away and pay what it costs in return for everything we import.
If this Government really wanted to do something, what it ought to do is to get together with the United States, Argentina and Australia which, combined, sell 95 per cent of the wheat and cereal crops, not to form a cartel or anything like that but to determine what the cost is of the production of the wheat which we give away to the rest of the world. Then we should arrive at an agreement, which may have to involve some production management and some schemes which would increase and decrease production. Then we could agree that no one would sell below that break even cost, and that break even cost would of course have to reflect the cost of production, including some return on the investment of the farmer, and the transportation costs.
After debating the Crow rate in the House for a year and a half, after we fought over who should get the subsidy and who should pay it and where it should go, we did not subsidize our farmers. We did not subsidize our railways. I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, whom we are subsidizing. We are subsidizing Russia, Japan and the European Economic Community, because they are the people to whom we are shipping our grain. We are exporting our cheap food after spending a year fighting over who pays and who receives a subsidy. Not once did the Minister mention that we are not really subsidizing any of our own producers or our own railways. The cost of transportation

May 3, 1984
Supply
is a cost of delivery and production of this most vital of our prime commodities, and we are giving it away.
Has the Minister talked to the United States, to Argentina or to Australia to see what they are doing, because they are in the same fix. I have gone to Washington with some of my colleagues and talked to some of our counterparts down there. They are saying, "What a great idea. We must do it. But every time we talk, because we are the leaders in the field, we get it in the neck from Canada because it will underbid us. It does not want to talk to us".
Has the Minister ever given any thought to producing a kind of policy which would give us a reasonable return? Of course, the rest of the world is saying, "What a cruel hoax that would be, to arrive at a supply-management agreement among the food producing countries when the whole world is starving for our food production", and that is quite true. Naturally, we should make a contribution to a world food bank. We should be responsible in terms of the unique position we are in and of our potential and ability to grow food. We should recognize also that there is great need for our production out in the world. Is it really the responsibility of the food producing countries only or should the other industrial countries make a contribution? What would a scheme look like which would involve all industrial countries, including the communist countries? They should make a contribution to a world bank which would be there in times of need so that millions of people would not starve to death from time to time in Africa, Asia and elsewhere. An ambulance driver should not ask whether he is going to get paid when he picks up an accident victim. What a cruel hoax it would be for an ambulance driver to say: Can you pay for the ride? But he has to be paid. He is not going to leave someone lying in the ditch, but eventually he has to be paid.
The same is true for a food-producing country. It cannot be the responsibility of the farmers only in countries like Canada, Australia and the United States to maintain a cheap food policy which permits domestic consumers a very privileged standard of living. It cannot be the responsibility of producing countries only to maintain a cheap food policy to feed the world. No, there has to be a broader responsibility.
What can we do? We can get together with our industrial partners in the world. There is a starving world out there. We have the capacity to produce but we need help to produce cheap food. There is no shortage of demand for our food in the rest of the world, but there is a shortage of demand for food with a price tag attached. We could commit ourselves to producing the necessary infrastructure, storage and handling facilities to get our food to places where it is needed. Then the other industrial countries such as Germany, France, Japan and others would pay into the food bank. They would then ask: What would it cost? Well, it costs us $4.50 or $6.50 to produce a bushel of wheat. That would reflect transportation costs and everything else. That would be the floor price. The other industrial countries would pay into the food bank, we would
control and manage it and we would have one crop year of wheat in our storage bins ready to be delivered anywhere in the world. But we cannot do it on our own.
I am asking this Minister, sitting there smiling and grinning in his condescending way, if he has ever thought about anything like that? Has he ever talked to the other industrial countries and asked them whether they accept the responsibility of feeding a hungry world? Or is he going to continue to dump the social responsibility we have to the underprivileged in our country and the rest of the world on to the backs of our farmers? That is his policy now, but it is high time for a change.

speechtext:
I just have a short comment, Mr. Speaker. I just wanted to say that we have discussed this many times with our trading partners. But the United States refuses to become involved in that kind of venture. I think it is most necessary. I have said many times that it is wrong for us to subsidize our producers because they do not have enough of a return to give them a decent living and we are supplying food to other countries at a price below the cost of production. Some of those other countries may not want to produce their own grain so long as we are going to continue that kind of system. The U.S. spent $15 billion or $20 billion this year purposely to interfere in the market system, trying to make the commodities scarce.
Both the Hon. Member and I know that in Canada we have a system which is old, but it guarantees a year's supply of stocks on hand which will supply the market in an orderly fashion. I discussed that with the Minister of Agriculture of France, Michel Rocard, this week. I am really surprised, but happy, to see a Conservative suggesting this kind of a controlled marketing system, bringing order in the marketplace. I am very happy and it has been worthwhile listening to the Hon. Member.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I found it fascinating to listen to this debate today. The first thing I want to say is that it would not have been necessary to move this kind of motion had the Government learned anything from the difficulties experienced in agriculture over the last 15 years. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) was in this House when we dealt with the first grain stabilization Bill in 1970-71. At that time there were some Liberal Members of Parliament from western Canada. I invite the Minister, who sends out more speeches than any other Minister, to get his speech writers to do a little research into the record of debates. I also invite him to talk to his colleague at suppertime instead of doing so while I am speaking.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext: They do not understand, so they will explain to each other.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I invite the Minister to talk to the former Member of Parliament for The Battlefords, Cliff
May 3, 1984

Mclsaac, and find out what he had to say about the western grain stabilization Bill in 1970-71, and the second Bill in 1974, 1975 and 1976.
In his press release the Minister said something about basing payments or triggering payments on cash flow. I and other Members of the House, Mr. Speaker, moved amendments on both grain stabilization Bills starting in 1971 to have the payments based on net income, not gross income. Well, he learned that much, but I want to remind him that he had better have two or three other amendments in his Bill, if and when he puts it in front of us, so that payments should be based not only on an overall basis but on a regional basis in the Canadian Wheat Board district. They could also be made out according to an individual crop.
The Bill is designed to protect the grain producers' income according to what the market is doing. Crop insurance will protect them from the weather and this legislation is supposed to protect them from the market. It is a double-barrelled operation. When we suggested that the payments should be made according to individual crops, as and when their prices fluctuate, the Government of the day, the then Minister of Transport, told us that we were getting into crop insurance. I invite the Hon. Minister of Agriculture to stay in the House and to check Hansard from 1970 to 1975.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext: A point of order, Mr. Speaker. I really want to stay and hear the Hon. Member but I have to catch an airplane. He can rest assured I will read Hansard and the great contribution I know he is going to make.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must include in my comments a mention of the efforts made by many Members of the House to get a grain income stabilization program to protect grain producers from the fluctuations of the world market. To expect producers to bear the burden by themselves in competition with the treasuries of our competitors is totally unfair. The nation as a whole should share those costs.
I listened to a number of candidates for the leadership of the Conservative Party last year, Mr. Speaker. I am now suffering through listening to seven Liberal candidates for the leadership of their Party this year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext: You will not be disappointed this time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
I hear them saying they are going to come up with new ideas. Well, what is wrong with the old ones since they have never been implemented? Old ideas such as, to quote Mr. Diefenbaker, parity, not charity. Old ones from the 1940s, 1950s and 1960s: price related to the cost of production plus a decent living. What is wrong with those old ideas? They have never been implemented. Let us blow the dust off them and do it. The legislation, if and when we get it, must include additional amendments to those the Minister has proposed in his press release, which none of them want to announce in Parliament. They want to do it somewhere out in the hills.
Supply
I heard the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) and other Members talk about higher freight rates. That is amusing, ironic and disgusting. This Party brought in legislation to raise the freight rates for farmers and forced it through. The ink was hardly dry on the legislation when a former Minister of Transport, executive vice-president of James Richardson and Sons, went out to Regina a week ago and cried about these poor grain producers having to pay higher freight rates and higher fuel taxes as a result of a Conservative budget in Saskatchewan. Where the heck was he last year? Mr. Lang was one of the leading spokesmen to erect the statutory grain rates and cause farmers to pay higher freight charges. The Tories are the ones who agreed with the Liberals that the Crow rate had to go and freight rates must go up. I agree that they said it should not be done today but, rather two or three years down the road. That is like cutting the dog's tail off one inch at a time instead of all at once. They both supported higher freight rates for grain producers, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext: So did you.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
I do not know what happened to the old idea of parity, not charity, of prices related to the cost of production plus a decent living. Mr. Speaker, they have had parity all right. Since World War II there has been parity for banks, lenders and large corporations. They get their cost of production and profits. However, if it is a grain producer, a fisherman, a little storekeeper, or a lower middle income homeowner, they must tough it out and tighten their belts. They must show restraint.
Our agricultural producers cannot compete in a world market in terms of exports or imports unless this nation as a whole will commit the finances necessary to make sure they survive. There was a famous episode in the Parliament of the United Kingdom when Mr. Churchill brought in a reduction in the rations on coal and fish. Aneurin Bevan said to the then Prime Minister that England was an island of coal surrounded by a sea of fish and only the organizational genius of the Government could see to it that they have a shortage of both. It has only been due to the organizational genius of successive national governments in this place that we have lost three quarters of a million farmers across Canada since 1950. This wild rush to bigger-is-better and to make sure that banks do all right has resulted in the Farm Credit Corporation being nothing more than a lender of last resort at rates that are as high or higher than banks charge.
The Western Grain Stabilization Act needs to be dealt with quickly, Mr. Speaker. We can assure the Government that it can go through all stages in three days at the most. I am sure the Senate will need only a couple of hours when it comes to doing some work. When it comes to leisure, they can take weeks, but when it comes to doing some work, they will deal with it in a couple of hours. We can have Royal Assent on the evening of the third day. I will be willing to remain here for an extra hour if necessary. However, the amendment had better

May 3, 1984
Supply
include payments being triggered not only on a net income but based on a regional basis and on individual crops.
I hope the one farmer who is left sitting over there will ask the Minister to renew and reopen the ability to opt in and out under the revised grain stabilization Bill. The 25 per cent or more of the grain producers who opted out were smart. They realized that it is going to be four, five, six or more years before there is another pay-out. Most of them are ahead of the game. They would have liked to have come into the plan, but they saw what the plan would involve. It is like some insurance policies. You must be struck by lightning at high noon in front of the city hall on a Tuesday next year in order to collect. That is what was wrong with the grain stabilization Bill. The ability to opt in or out must be revised and updated. The Minister must include those additional amendments in the legislation. He had better table it for first reading and get going on second reading by next Tuesday or Wednesday.
The next item in the motion, Mr. Speaker, deals with the repeal of fuel taxes. As I mentioned earlier, the former Minister of Transport, the guy who helped kill the Crow rate, is crying because of the increased fuel taxes on railroads meaning higher freight rates for farmers. He was right. The headlines of recent weeks say that the new freight rates starting August 1 will be higher than expected. They are going to be higher than expected every year until 1991, Mr. Speaker. I hate people who say, "I told you so", but I did tell you so last year and the year before and the year before that. I hope that people on the Government side will believe me now. Mr. Speaker, those kinds of taxes on primary production are totally out of place, whether on farmers, fishermen or forest products. If we need to raise revenue we should raise it through our general tax system for all citizens based on ability to pay and based on the taxable income they earn, no matter how they earned it.
An immediate interest rate reduction requires that we do some of the things which Mr. St. Laurent did during the Korean War and which Mr. Diefenbaker did in 1959 and 1960. Sometimes they were ridiculed for it. They pegged the dollar and the interest rates and put on foreign exchange controls. They did not worry about what our dollar was worth compared to the American dollar. The issue is what our dollar is worth to us in Canada and what it is doing for us here. I do not know if my colleagues in my own caucus would agree with me, but I personally hope the Canadian dollar goes down some more compared to the American dollar. That is great for our exports.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR FARMERS
speechtext: Exactly.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-ALLOCATION OF FOOD PROVIDED BY VANCOUVER FOOD BANK. (B) BENEFITS OF ECONOMIC RECOVERY. (C) PRODUCTIVITY INCREASE-EFFECT ON EMPLOYMENT
LABOUR CONDITIONS-ALLOCATION OF FOOD PROVIDED BY VANCOUVER FOOD BANK. (B) BENEFITS OF ECONOMIC RECOVERY. (C) PRODUCTIVITY INCREASE-EFFECT ON EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is an economic emergency in my home province of British Columbia. I would like Members of the House of Commons to know about it.
Recently in the House I told the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) during Question Period that there was a record number of people making use of the Vancouver food bank. Now local newspapers in my riding, such as the South Vancouver Review, the Highland Echo, and the East-Ender, to name three, are reporting that people are being turned away from the food bank. What a terrible situation it is in 1984 to have food banks to feed poor people.
In The Globe and Mail for Saturday, April 28, 1984, the headline read "B.C. employment level highest since Depression." It reported that 39.5 per cent, almost 40 per cent, of young people between the ages of 15 and 19 in British Columbia are unemployed and that 25.9 per cent of those between the ages of 20 to 24 are also without jobs. Those figures are surpassed only by Newfoundland parts of New Brunswick and West Virginia, areas which are notoriously depressed areas in North America.
May 3, 1984

I think that British Columbia must be declared a national emergency area. An emergency federal-provincial meeting must be held. I urge the Minister of Finance to meet personally with Premier Bill Bennett as soon as possible. B.C. has already qualified for the First time in its history for a fiscal stabilization grant. That means British Columbia for the first time is a have-not province.
We need more federal initiatives than this for Western Canada economic development. For example, in forestry we could use emergency funds right now in the short-term for tree planting. That would put some of the young people to work this summer. In the long-term we have to replenish our resource base in British Columbia. Tree planting would help that. In fisheries we need more federal funds for salmonid enhancement to improve our Fishstocks. We need more environmentally sensitive economic planning.
We are also hurting in British Columbia because of our provincial government. Many of my constituents are afraid that come the next federal election, we have Brian Mulroney or John Turner as Prime Minister, we will see Premier Bill Bennett's policies on the federal level. There has been much talk of turning B.C. into a high-tech area like Japan. While I am in favour of high-tech, in facing the future we have to be careful. Our real strength is in our resources in Western Canada and in British Columbia. A wise person would say concentrate on your strengths, concentrate on your resources.
We need in the longer term a regional plan for Western Canada to get our economy back on track. Our industries are resource based, they are cyclical; for example, Fishing, mining, forestry, agriculture, oil and gas. These resources are being gutted right now by federal and provincial inaction. Our future is being sold and we will be left with nothing. We are losing our forests. We are losing our fish stocks. Our agriculture is being threatened by a provincial government which will not live with the agricultural land freeze. We need a sector by sector approach to deal with Western economic development. That is the real way to develop the West.
We should look at the Pacific Rim for markets. We should have an Asia-PaciFic Foundation as soon as possible. We should look to education and training of our young people so that we can develop industries in British Columbia. We should diversify our economy through secondary industries in British Columbia. We have to improve our labour relations as well. I think I know of a way whereby we could do that. We should stress worker ownership which would reduce unemployment and inflation. There would be less capital flight and less alienation among our workers. There would be greater productivity and greater competitiveness. Finally, we should look for regional marketing and ways to get people to reinvest their proFits in British Columbia.
There is a national emergency in my province. Surely in 1984 people should not have to go to food banks. We in the NDP have a proud tradition; we are and have been advocates of the ordinary people. Now, more than ever, we are deter-
Adjournment Debate
mined that people in British Columbia will obtain jobs and not have to go to food banks to get their daily necessities.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-ALLOCATION OF FOOD PROVIDED BY VANCOUVER FOOD BANK. (B) BENEFITS OF ECONOMIC RECOVERY. (C) PRODUCTIVITY INCREASE-EFFECT ON EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) questioned where the economic recovery in Canada was going and asked who was getting the benefits of the recovery. He particularly zeroed in on the problems in British Columbia. Fie mentioned tree planting and unemployment.
I should like to indicate that the federal Government has already taken steps to put the unemployed people of that province back to work. I will just refer to one example, the Environment 2000 program, into which we are putting funding because the province was not doing it. That is not only the case with British Columbia but with other provinces as well. I worked on that particular program because I realized how the forests were being ravaged and that no replacement planning was taking place, not only to provide for future forests but also to maintain the spawning beds of fish in the streams and rivers. I am pleased that the Government of Canada has been able to assist in this sector.
In the budget forecast, real GNE is expected to increase 4.9 per cent in 1984 or roughly about 1 per cent real growth per quarter. This represents a moderating pace of economic growth compared with the very strong real growth obtained in the first four quarters of the recovery. This pattern is typical of economic cycles in Canada.
This economic growth is projected to be accompanied by a stable inflation rate of about 5 per cent in the near-term, followed by further modest reductions over the medium-term. The rebound in productivity growth which was first witnessed in 1983 after nearly a decade of lacklustre activity performance in Canada is expected to continue in 1984 and beyond. This sharp movement in productivity growth, combined with a consolidation of Canada's hard-won gains on the inflation and cost fronts, will serve to improve Canada's competitive position internationally and lay the framework for sustained, non-inflationary real income growth in Canada over the medium-term.
Some further economic data have become available since the Budget. While month to month movements in economic indicators are always very volatile, the information to date indicates that the economic recovery in Canada is continuing. This view is shared by Canadian forecasters. The most recent survey of real growth prospects by the Conference Board indicated that Canadian private sector forecasters are looking for an average 4.4 per cent real growth throughout 1984.
Here are the facts. Compared with the levels of a year ago, average real Gross Domestic Product for January and February was up 6.1 per cent. Over this period industrial production has risen 12.8 per cent and retail sales are up 5.6 per cent in real terms.
Since the final quarter of 1983, employment increased 0.2 per cent in the First quarter of this year. The unemployment rate for March, 1984 is 1.1 per cent below the rate of one year earlier. Housing starts remain rather low, averaging 145,000

May 3, 1984
Adjournment Debate
units over the first quarter. A record trade balance of $25.2 billion was recorded in January, although the figure fell to $13.7 billion in February. On average, over recent months the trade picture has been very strong. There has been a sharp deceleration in inflation. The year over year increase in March, 1984 was down to 4.7 per cent.
The Hon. Member asked who was benefiting from this recovery. Clearly all Canadians benefit from an economy that is growing and creating jobs, that is registering large increases in productivity and that is becoming more competitive. The financial health of the corporate sector is rapidly being repaired and in foreign markets Canadian companies are increasingly competitive. These trends are reinforced by the favourable improvements in productivity and production costs in Canada. These developments will continue to generate more jobs for Canadians and encourage new investment in business plant and equipment.

subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT-REQUEST FOR EARLY INTRODUCTION OF AMENDING LEGISLATION.
WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT-REQUEST FOR EARLY INTRODUCTION OF AMENDING LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a concern which I want to raise with the Parliamentary Secretary this evening. It goes back to a question on April 18, the last question in the House before we went home for the Easter break. I asked the question of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) who at that time answered in the House in areas connected with the Western Grain Stabilization Act. Those areas have been well talked about. They were talked about today in the Opposition debate on agriculture.
We have a simple straightforward legislative measure designed to stabilize income from grain in the Wheat Board area, the three Prairie Provinces plus the Peace River country. It is designed on the basis of a dollar contribution from the producers to be matched by $2 from the Government. The formula in place is supposed to make payouts when income on the Prairies from the sale of grain falls below certain averages.
Anybody with vision, able to hear and think, has to know that that formula is not working the way it was intended. We are not being critical of the Government because when the Bill was brought forward in 1976 or 1977 it did not have the correct formula. We understand that it was not necessarily right at the time. In hindsight, things could have been done differently. We are talking about today. The Bill was passed by this House. It did not fall from Heaven like a tablet of stone, in which case it would be tough to argue and amend. It was made in this place and is capable of being changed or amended in this place.
The NDP and the Official Opposition both agreed to cooperate with the Government and pass amendments that would provide much needed cash to western producers as quickly as possible. We agreed to that. We on this side have indicated our concern for well over a year, back to February or March, 1983. We are asking that the Government come to its
senses and begin to spread around some of the money available through this fund.
A question I had on the Order Paper which was answered on January 27 of this year simply asked the amount of money in the fund at the end of December, 1983. I will place that figure on the record. It is $864,091,918.74; $864 million. The fund had built up to such a level it was considered enough of a nestegg to protect the solvency of the fund against any possible or future drawdowns. The fund was at such a level that it triggered an automatic reduction in the amount of premium the producer was paying. The producer's levy went from 2 per cent of his gross sales to 1.5 per cent. That is a clear indication that there was a lot of money in the fund.
Everybody knows that there are financial problems on the Prairies, of many kinds and in record numbers. I do not want to be dramatic and talk about this being similar to the thirties, but there are as many financial problems on the Prairies as at any time since the 1930s. On the one hand we have a measure that creates a fund which grows to such an extent that the contribution to increase that fund is decreased by a triggering mechanism. On the other hand, we have producers in financial trouble. There does not seem to be any interim mechanism so that we can get that money to producers and spread it around.
We on this side have offered to co-operate with the Government. In February, the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) moved a motion in the Committee on Agriculture encouraging the the Government to do something. We showed support there. When the Minister responsible in the other place appeared before the committee on February 13 he said the problem was mentioned in the December, 1983 Throne Speech and it was his hope they would be presenting amendments during the session which would improve the responsiveness of the program and increase its acceptability to producers. That was in February. It is a simple measure, there is co-operation from the Opposition, producers have financial problems, money is available at least to address some of the problems of producers, and yet nothing happens. What do we get? We received a fancy press kit which was issued in Winnipeg a week ago yesterday. It does nothing. It is really only an essay indicating what the Government intends to do.
The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) who just spoke said the Government does not want to do anything in the House. This is a clear example of that. We have been encouraging the Government to do things in the House and what do we get? We get a press release that was made outside the House telling people what the Government intends to do. What we need is action. The press release did not do anything. We have not seen any legislation. Even if we go along with the Government's intentions, nothing will happen until the fall. There is absolutely no reason why we could not make an interim payment, and there is absolutely no reason why we could not make that payment within two weeks. We could do that if the will to do so existed.
May 3, 1984

There are all kinds of electronic systems in place for mailing and for putting money into circulation. I believe there are several millions of cheques that go in the mail each month to various recipients across the country. This payment would involve something like over 100,000 cheques. That would be no problem at all as far as our capacity to put things in the mail is concerned.
What I do not understand is why the Government is in fact delaying this. The latest thing I have heard is that the Government intends to introduce a Bill in the Senate. If that in fact is the case, it is another indication that the Government has no intention of addressing this matter on an urgent basis. If it wants to get a Bill through quickly, it should bring it into the House where we will deal with it very quickly, and then it will go to the Senate. If it goes to the Senate, the Bill must first go through the Senate committee system. As a rule, we in the House do not pre-study Bills. If the Bill goes to Senate, it will further delay its implementation at a very, very critical time. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will stand and announce when the Bill will be presented so that we in the House may in fact do something to support farmers at an extremely critical time of the year.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Bachand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT-REQUEST FOR EARLY INTRODUCTION OF AMENDING LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer), I am happy to announce that legislation to amend the Western Grain Stabilization Act will be introduced in Parliament in the very near future. In fact, the text of this legislation is now ready, and, to my knowledge, it now is or will be the subject of discussions between the House Leaders this week.
We want to thank the Members of the Official Opposition for supporting quick passage of the amendments which will be submitted for parliamentary approval. It is good to know that the Official Opposition agrees with us on the need to amend this Act as soon as possible to make it more flexible and better suited to the needs of western farmers. The Western Grain Stabilization Act is the main federal program aimed at protecting the income of Prairie grain growers.
Adjournment Debate
However, this program must be amended, especially to provide better protection to producers against sudden fluctuations in prices and costs during the periods when increased volumes are being marketed. We therefore propose to add a unitary readjustment payment for making cash available to ensure that the program will be better suited to the financial situation of participating grain growers during the periods when production and the volume marketed are increasing.
For instance, under the present stabilization payment formula, no payment would be made for the calendar year ending December 31, 1983. However, if the recommended amendments are approved, a substantial payment of over $3 million could be made for the crop year ending July 31, 1984. Other amendments are also being considered following the recommendations of the Producers' Advisory Committee of the Western Grain Growers' Income Stabilization Administration and other organizations of the farming and grain-growing industries.
Among the amendments suggested, there is a recommendation that the program application period coincide with the crop year so that a closer relationship may be established between the income from a given crop and the production costs incurred for this same crop.
Two other measures providing for the participation of eligible spouses and the possibility for participants to withdraw from the program every ten years will eliminate some of the discriminatory provisions of the existing legislation.
It is obvious therefore that the rationale behind the program is not being questioned. The sole purpose of the proposed amendments is to make the system more flexible, to the benefit of Prairie wheat growers.
With the support of the Opposition, the new program will soon become a reality.
